weeks.title: What a website actually is
weeks.context:
A website is a set of files. When you type a URL in a browser, the browser makes an HTTP request to a server, the server sends back files, and the browser interprets those files and renders them on screen. Understanding this at the file level, without build tools, frameworks, or abstractions, is where every web developer's understanding should start. You can only choose the right tools when you understand what problem they solve.

HTML describes the structure and content of a page: what the heading says, where the paragraphs are, which text is a link, what the images are. CSS describes how it looks: colours, spacing, fonts, layout. This separation of concerns is not just convention, it is what allows a graphic designer to change the visual style of a page without touching the content, and a content editor to add new text without touching the layout code.

Bean Forge v0.1 is a one-page website for a fictional coffee shop. It has a header, a menu section, an about section, and a footer. It looks good on mobile and on desktop. And it is built with nothing but HTML, CSS, and a text editor. No npm, no React, no webpack. The point is not that this is how professionals work, it is that by the end of this week, you understand exactly what happens when a browser loads a page, because you wrote every byte of it.

CSS layout has two modern systems worth understanding: flexbox and grid. Flexbox distributes items along one axis (a row or column of navigation links, a row of feature cards). Grid distributes items on two axes simultaneously (a page layout with header, sidebar, main content, and footer). They are complementary, not competing, most pages use both. Mobile-first design means writing CSS for small screens first, then adding media queries for larger screens. This is the correct direction: most web traffic is now mobile, and it is easier to scale up a simple layout than to scale down a complex one.

Deploying to Netlify takes 5 minutes for a static HTML site. Create a repo, push the files, connect to Netlify, and you have a live public URL with HTTPS. This week ends with a URL you can share.

items.title: What Node.js is and why you need it
items.body:
## What Node.js is
Node.js lets you run JavaScript outside a browser, on your laptop, on a server, anywhere. Every tool in this track (npm, Next.js, Prisma, etc.) runs on Node.js. Without it, nothing works.

## What you'll do today
1. Install Node.js from nodejs.org (LTS version)
2. Install VS Code from code.visualstudio.com
3. Verify installations: `node --version`, `npm --version`
4. Write `hello.js` with `console.log("Hello Forge")`
5. Run it: `node hello.js`

## Why before anything else
Every React component, every API endpoint, every build script you write this track runs through Node.js. Get this right once and you're set for 24 weeks.

items.title: How the web works
items.body:
## A website is just files a browser fetches
Before any framework or build tool, understand the bedrock: **a website is a set of files**, and the web is a request for those files. When you type a URL, your browser makes an **HTTP request** to a server, the server sends back files (HTML, CSS, images), and the browser interprets and renders them on screen. That is the entire model, and understanding it at the file level, with no abstractions, is where every web developer's understanding should begin, because you can only choose the right tools later when you understand the raw problem they solve.
```text
you type a URL ->  browser sends HTTP REQUEST to a server
                   server sends back FILES (html, css, js, images) = HTTP RESPONSE
                   browser interprets the files and renders the page
```

## The three languages, and why they are separate
A web page is built from three languages, each with one job, and the separation is deliberate and important:
- **HTML** describes **structure and content**: what is a heading, where the paragraphs are, which text is a link, what the images are. It is the *what*.
- **CSS** describes **appearance**: colours, spacing, fonts, layout. It is the *how it looks*.
- **JavaScript** (next week) adds **behaviour**: responding to clicks and input. The *what it does*.
This **separation of concerns** is not just tidiness, it is what lets a designer change the visual style (CSS) without touching the content, and a content editor add text (HTML) without touching the layout, the two can work independently because the content and the styling live in different places. Keeping structure (HTML) and presentation (CSS) separate is a foundational discipline you carry through every framework that follows, even when tools blur the line, the mental model stays: content is one thing, styling is another.

## What you'll build: Bean Forge
This track is built around one project you grow for 24 weeks: **Bean Forge**, a website for a fictional coffee shop. **v0.1** this week is a one-page site, real HTML and CSS, no frameworks, that looks good, works on phones, and is *deployed to a public URL* anyone can visit. Starting with raw HTML/CSS (not a framework) is deliberate: you learn what a web page fundamentally *is* before you learn the tools that abstract it, so that when you reach React and Next.js later, you understand what they are doing *for* you rather than treating them as magic. By Sunday, Bean Forge v0.1 is live on the internet, and you have done, by hand, the thing every framework automates.

## Where this fits
This opens the **Foundations phase** (W1-4), where Bean Forge grows from a static page to an interactive, form-handling, component-based site: v0.1 raw HTML/CSS this week, then JavaScript interactivity (W2), a working contact form (W3), and a refactor to the Astro framework (W4). Starting at the file level is the foundation for everything: the frontend, backend, and production phases all build on understanding that the web is requests for files that a browser renders. Today's orientation: a website is files fetched over HTTP, built from HTML (structure), CSS (style), and JS (behaviour), kept separate by design, and you will build Bean Forge from the ground up. Tomorrow you set up your editor and write the HTML skeleton.

items.title: Style it with CSS
items.body:
## Style it with CSS
With the structure in place, you style Bean Forge with **CSS**, which works by *selecting* elements and applying visual rules to them:
```css
/* selector { property: value; } */
body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; color: #2b2b2b; margin: 0; }
.hero { background: #6f4e37; color: white; padding: 4rem 1.5rem; text-align: center; }
.menu-item { border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 8px; padding: 1rem; }
```
You write CSS in a separate `.css` file (linked from the HTML's `<head>`), keeping style separate from structure (the separation of concerns again). Each rule has a **selector** (which elements, by tag, class `.menu-item`, or id `#hero`) and **declarations** (the property/value pairs that set how they look).

## The two ideas that make CSS make sense: the box model and layout
Two concepts unlock most of CSS, and confusion about them is the source of most beginner frustration:
- **The box model:** *every* element is a rectangular box with four layers from inside out, **content**, **padding** (space inside, between content and border), **border**, and **margin** (space outside, between this element and others). Most "why is there a gap / why is this too big?" confusion is the box model, and `box-sizing: border-box` (which makes width include padding and border) is the one setting that makes sizing behave intuitively, set it on everything.
- **Layout (Flexbox and Grid):** how you arrange elements in rows and columns. **Flexbox** (`display: flex`) lays items in a row or column with easy alignment and spacing, perfect for a nav bar or a row of cards; **Grid** (`display: grid`) makes two-dimensional layouts. These replaced the old hacks (floats, tables) and are how all modern layout is done.
```css
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
.menu { display: flex; gap: 1rem; flex-wrap: wrap; }   /* a responsive row of items */
```
Understanding the box model (spacing) and Flexbox/Grid (arrangement) is most of practical CSS.

## CSS is about consistency, not magic numbers
A discipline that separates clean CSS from a mess: build with a **consistent system**, not arbitrary one-off values. Define a small set of colours (Bean Forge's coffee browns, a cream, a dark text) and reuse them, ideally as CSS custom properties (variables) so a colour change is one edit:
```css
:root { --coffee: #6f4e37; --cream: #f5f0e8; --ink: #2b2b2b; }
.hero { background: var(--coffee); }
```
Use consistent spacing (multiples of a base, like 0.5rem, 1rem, 1.5rem) rather than random pixel values, and consistent fonts. This consistency is what makes a site look *designed* rather than thrown together, and it previews the "design system" idea you will formalise with Tailwind in W7. The beginner trap is sprinkling magic numbers (`margin: 13px` here, `17px` there, five slightly-different blues), which produces a subtly off, inconsistent look; reusing a defined palette and spacing scale produces coherence for free. Style with a system, and the page looks professional.

## Where this fits
You styled Bean Forge with CSS: selectors and declarations in a separate file, the box model (with `border-box`) for spacing, Flexbox/Grid for layout, and a consistent colour-and-spacing system (via CSS variables) for a designed look. The site now looks good on a desktop. Tomorrow you make it work on phones, where most visitors actually are.

days.title: Make it work on phones

items.title: Make it work on phones
items.body:
## Make it work on phones
Most web traffic is on phones, so a site that only looks good on a desktop is broken for the majority of visitors. **Responsive design** makes a page adapt to any screen size, and it starts with one tag you already added in W1, the **viewport meta tag**, which tells the phone to render at its real width instead of pretending to be a zoomed-out desktop:
```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
```
Without it, your carefully-styled page renders tiny and zoomed-out on phones, the single most common "my site looks broken on mobile" cause. With it, the page uses the phone's actual width, and your responsive CSS can adapt the layout.

## Media queries and fluid layout
You adapt the layout to screen size with **media queries**, CSS rules that apply only at certain widths, combined with already-flexible layout:
```css
.menu { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 1rem; }  /* phone: stacked */
@media (min-width: 700px) {
  .menu { flex-direction: row; flex-wrap: wrap; }            /* wider: side by side */
}
```
The modern, recommended approach is **mobile-first**: write the base CSS for the small screen (the simplest, stacked layout), then use `min-width` media queries to *add* complexity as the screen gets wider. This is better than the reverse because the phone layout is usually the simplest (everything in one column), so starting there and progressively enhancing for bigger screens produces cleaner CSS and ensures the mobile experience, the one most users get, is the priority rather than an afterthought. You also use fluid, flexible units (percentages, `rem`, `flex-wrap`, `max-width`) so layouts *stretch* rather than break, a `max-width` on the content plus `flex-wrap` on a row of cards handles a huge range of sizes with no media query at all.

## Test on real (or simulated) phones
The discipline that makes responsive design actually work is **testing at multiple sizes**, not assuming. Open your browser's developer tools (F12) and use the device-toolbar / responsive mode to view the page at phone, tablet, and desktop widths, and *also* check it on a real phone if you can (the deployed URL from D6 makes this easy). You are looking for the things that break at small sizes: text overflowing, images too wide, a nav that does not fit, touch targets (buttons, links) too small to tap. The common failures are predictable, a fixed-width element wider than the phone (causing horizontal scroll), tap targets too close together, text that needs zooming, and you fix them with the fluid units and media queries above. Designing and testing responsively is not optional polish; it is core correctness, because a site that fails on phones fails for most of its audience, and "it looked fine on my laptop" is exactly how broken-on-mobile sites ship.

## Where this fits
You made Bean Forge responsive: the viewport tag so phones render correctly, mobile-first media queries and fluid layout that adapt the design to any screen, and testing across sizes to catch what breaks. The site now works for the phone-majority of visitors. Tomorrow you add the first touches of interactivity with simple links, click-to-call and a map.

items.title: Add click-to-call and map link
items.body: ## Add click-to-call and a map link A coffee shop site has a job: get people to visit or call, so you add the two most useful real-world links, **click-to-call** (tap the phone number, the phone dials it) and a **map link** (tap the address, it opens in maps). These need no JavaScript, just special URL schemes in `` tags, which is a nice lesson that links are more capable than they first appear: ```html (202) 555-0173 123 Roast Ave Email us ``` On a phone, `tel:` triggers the dialer and a maps URL opens the maps app, exactly the frictionless "tap to act" behaviour that turns a visitor into a customer. ## Why these small touches matter These links seem trivial, but they teach a real product lesson: **meet the user's actual goal with the least friction.** Someone visiting a coffee shop's site on their phone most likely wants to *call*, *find*, or *email* the shop, and making each of those a single tap (rather than forcing them to copy the number, switch apps, and paste) removes friction at exactly the moments that convert interest into a visit. This is the difference between a site that merely *displays* information and one that is *useful*, and it costs almost nothing to build. It also reinforces that good web development is about the user's real-world job, not just the technology, the `tel:` link is simple, but knowing to add it shows you are thinking about what the visitor actually needs to *do*. Small, thoughtful touches like these are a large part of what makes a site feel professional and considered. ## Accessibility and correctness of links While adding links, build the habits that make them correct and accessible: - **Descriptive link text:** the link's text should make sense on its own, "Call (202) 555-0173" or "123 Roast Ave," not "click here," because screen-reader users often navigate by jumping between links and need each to be self-explanatory, and "click here" tells them nothing. - **External links:** links that leave your site (the map) can open in a new tab with `target="_blank"`, and when you do, add `rel="noopener noreferrer"` (a small security and performance safeguard for `_blank` links). - **Real, working destinations:** double-check the actual phone number, address, and email, a click-to-call link to a wrong number is worse than no link. These are small correctness-and-accessibility habits, but building them now means every link you write for the rest of your career is descriptive, safe, and works, which is exactly the kind of quietly-good default that distinguishes a careful developer. Links are the web's most fundamental interaction, and getting them right, useful, accessible, correct, is foundational. ## Where this fits You added click-to-call, map, and email links to Bean Forge, frictionless single-tap actions that serve the visitor's real goals, built with descriptive accessible link text and safe external-link handling. The site is now genuinely useful, not just informative. Tomorrow you put it on the public internet by pushing to GitHub and deploying on Netlify.

days.title: Push to GitHub and deploy on Netlify
days.summary: Today you put it ONLINE. A real public URL.

items.title: Push to GitHub and deploy on Netlify
items.body:
## Put it on the internet: GitHub + Netlify
A site on your laptop helps no one, so today Bean Forge goes live. Two steps: push your code to **GitHub** (version control + a home for the code), then connect **Netlify** to deploy it to a public URL automatically. First, version and push:
```bash
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Bean Forge v0.1: responsive coffee shop site"
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOU/bean-forge.git
git push -u origin main
```
Then on Netlify: connect your GitHub repo, and Netlify builds and serves your site at a public URL (like `bean-forge.netlify.app`). For a static HTML/CSS site there is nothing to build, Netlify just serves your files, and your coffee shop is live on the internet.

## Why this workflow is the foundation of modern deployment
This GitHub-plus-Netlify setup is not just a way to get a URL, it is the **continuous deployment** workflow that underlies all modern web development, and learning it now pays off all track. The key property: once connected, **every push to GitHub automatically redeploys the site.** You change Bean Forge, commit, push, and seconds later the live site updates, no manual uploading, no FTP, no copying files to a server. This is the same automated deploy-on-push that you will formalise as CI/CD later (W19), and experiencing it now, on a simple static site, builds the right mental model: your git repository is the source of truth, and deployment is an automatic consequence of pushing to it. It also means your *workflow* is the professional one from day one, work locally, commit meaningful changes, push, and the live site follows, which is exactly how real teams ship. The fact that it works this smoothly for a static site is a gift; the same pattern scales to the most complex apps.

## Deployment makes the work real
Beyond the mechanics, getting Bean Forge live is what makes the work *real* and is a habit to build deeply: a site that is deployed is a site that exists, that you can share, that you can test on a real phone, that is a portfolio piece. The discipline of *shipping early and often*, deploying v0.1 now rather than waiting until the site is "perfect", is one of the most valuable in web development, because a live site surfaces real issues (it loads slowly, it breaks on an actual phone, a link is wrong) that you would never catch locally, and because a shipped simple thing is worth infinitely more than an unshipped elaborate one. You will deploy every version of Bean Forge as you build it (v0.1 now, v0.2, v0.3, v0.4...), building both the project's public history and the habit of finishing and shipping work. Getting something live, then improving it in the open, is the rhythm of real web development, and starting it at v0.1 sets exactly the right pattern.

## Where this fits
Bean Forge v0.1 is live on a public URL via GitHub and Netlify, with the continuous-deployment workflow (push to GitHub, auto-redeploy) that underlies all modern web development, and the ship-early habit that makes work real. Your coffee shop site is on the internet. Tomorrow you polish it and write documentation, completing v0.1.

items.title: Polish and document
items.body:
## Polish and document v0.1
The site works and is live; today you polish the rough edges and document it, the finishing that turns a working page into a professional one. Polish is the small stuff that collectively makes a site feel considered: consistent spacing, aligned elements, a favicon (the little icon in the browser tab), proper page `<title>` and meta description (for search results and link previews), readable contrast, and no obvious glitches at any screen size. Walk through the live site critically, on desktop and phone, and fix what looks off, this critical pass is itself a skill, learning to *see* the details that separate amateur from professional.

## Document so others (and future-you) understand it
Write a **README** for the repo, the project's front door, that explains what Bean Forge is, how to run it locally, and where it is deployed:
```text
# Bean Forge
A responsive website for Bean Forge, a specialty coffee shop.
Built with plain HTML and CSS (no frameworks) as v0.1.

## Run locally
Open index.html in a browser, that's it.

## Deployed
https://bean-forge.netlify.app

## Versions
- v0.1 - responsive one-page site (HTML/CSS)
```
Documentation matters even for a simple project: a README is what lets a stranger (a potential employer, a collaborator, future-you) understand the project without reading all the code, and writing one is a habit that makes every project you build more credible and usable. Tag the release (`git tag v0.1`) so the version history begins.

## Why polish and docs are real work, not afterthoughts
The lesson of this first finishing day, which recurs through the whole track (culminating in W23, "the last 5% that takes 50% of the time"), is that **polish and documentation are core work, not optional extras.** The difference between a site that feels amateur and one that feels professional is rarely the big features, it is the accumulated small details: the consistent spacing, the favicon, the title that shows in search, the absence of glitches, the clear README. Users (and employers) notice this quality even when they cannot name it, a polished site signals care and competence, a rough one signals neither. Building the habit *now*, on a simple site, of finishing properly, polishing the details and documenting the work, rather than declaring victory the moment it technically functions, is what makes you a developer who ships *good* things, not just working ones. The 5% of polish genuinely does take a disproportionate share of the effort, and it is disproportionately what people remember, so treating it as real work from v0.1 is exactly the right standard to set.

## Where this fits
You polished Bean Forge v0.1 (consistent details, favicon, meta tags, no glitches) and documented it with a README and a version tag, the finishing that makes a site professional, with the habit that polish and docs are core work. Bean Forge v0.1 is complete: a responsive, useful, live, documented coffee shop site, built by hand from HTML and CSS. Next week you bring it to life with JavaScript, adding the interactivity, a daily special, menu filters, dark mode, that makes a page *respond* to the user.

weeks.title: Bean Forge v0.2: JavaScript interactivity
weeks.context:
HTML and CSS give you structure and style. JavaScript gives the page behavior, it responds to what the user does. When a user clicks a button, types in a search box, or toggles dark mode, JavaScript is what makes something happen without a full page reload. This week you add interactivity to Bean Forge: a daily special that changes based on the day, menu filters that show/hide items, and dark mode that remembers the user's preference across visits.

The Document Object Model (DOM) is JavaScript's interface to the page. Every HTML element, every div, paragraph, button, and image, is a node in the DOM tree. JavaScript can find any element (document.querySelector('.menu-item')), change its content (element.textContent = 'New text'), change its style (element.classList.add('hidden')), and listen for user actions (element.addEventListener('click', handler)). This is how dynamic behavior is created without sending new requests to a server.

Events are signals that user actions or browser state changes generate. A click event fires when the user clicks an element. An input event fires when the user types. A DOMContentLoaded event fires when the HTML has been parsed and the DOM is ready. Event listeners attach functions to these signals. The function receives an event object with details about what happened, which element was clicked, what key was pressed, the current value of an input field.

localStorage is a browser-provided key-value store that persists data between page visits. Unlike cookies, localStorage is never sent to the server and has no expiration date (until the user clears browser storage or you delete it explicitly). For user preferences that should persist, dark mode, language selection, form draft content, localStorage is the right tool. The API is simple: localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark'); and localStorage.getItem('theme').

The dark mode implementation teaches a complete pattern: check localStorage on page load and apply the saved theme, toggle the theme when the user clicks the button, and save the new preference to localStorage. Every user preference you implement in the future follows this same structure.

items.title: Today's special
items.body:
## Today's special: logic that responds to context
Your first real feature: a **daily special** that automatically shows a different coffee depending on the day of the week, so the site feels alive and current without anyone updating it. This combines JavaScript's logic (get the day, pick the matching special) with the DOM (display it on the page):
```js
const specials = ["Sunday Pour-Over", "Monday Mocha", "Tuesday Cortado",
                  "Wednesday Flat White", "Thursday Cold Brew",
                  "Friday Affogato", "Saturday Espresso Tonic"];
const today = new Date().getDay();            // 0=Sunday ... 6=Saturday
const special = specials[today];              // pick by index
document.querySelector('#special').textContent = special;   // show it
```
`new Date().getDay()` reads the visitor's current day, you use it as an index into the array of specials, and you write the result into the page. The site now shows the right special every day, automatically.

## What this small feature teaches
This modest feature packs in several patterns you will use constantly, which is why it is the first one:
- **Working with data and the DOM together:** you have *data* (the array of specials) and you *derive* something from it (today's), then *render* it to the page. Data in, logic, output to the DOM, the fundamental shape of dynamic web features, from this special to a full app rendering a list of products.
- **Reading dynamic context:** `new Date()` reads real-world state (the current day), so the page reflects the actual moment, your first taste of a page that *responds to the world*, not just to clicks.
- **Arrays and indexing:** picking `specials[today]` is array access by index, exactly the operation behind rendering any list-driven content.
It is a small feature, but it is a complete miniature of how dynamic content works: take data, apply logic, update the DOM, which scales directly to fetching products from a server and rendering them, or any data-driven interface.

## Guard against the edge cases
A discipline worth building from your very first feature: think about what could go *wrong* and handle it. Here, what if the `#special` element does not exist (a typo in the selector)? `querySelector` returns `null`, and `null.textContent = ...` throws an error that stops your script, the "Cannot read property of null" you met yesterday. A defensive habit:
```js
const el = document.querySelector('#special');
if (el) el.textContent = special;        // only set it if the element exists
```
More broadly, you ask: does the data cover all cases (an entry for every day, 0-6)? What if `getDay` returned something unexpected? Building the habit of *anticipating the broken case*, the missing element, the empty data, the unexpected value, rather than only coding the happy path, is what separates code that works in your demo from code that works for real users in situations you did not foresee. It is a small thing here (one `if`), but it is the start of the defensive mindset that matters enormously as features grow, because real users and real data will always find the edge case you ignored. Code the happy path *and* guard the edges.

## Where this fits
You built the daily-special feature, deriving content from data and the current day and rendering it to the DOM, the fundamental data-logic-render shape of dynamic content, with a first habit of guarding edge cases (the missing element). Tomorrow you build interactivity that responds to clicks: a menu filter.

items.title: Dark mode
Smooth scroll + animation
items.body: ## Smooth scroll and tasteful animation Today you add motion, smooth scrolling for in-page navigation and subtle animations, the polish that makes a site feel refined and alive. Smooth scrolling (clicking "Menu" glides down to the menu section instead of jumping) is almost free: ```css html { scroll-behavior: smooth; } /* CSS handles smooth anchor scrolling */ ``` ```html Menu ``` And subtle entrance animations (menu items fading in as you scroll to them) use CSS transitions/animations, optionally triggered by JavaScript when an element scrolls into view: ```css .menu-item { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(20px); transition: all 0.4s ease; } .menu-item.visible { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); } /* JS adds .visible on scroll-in */ ``` ## Why CSS does the animation, JavaScript just triggers it The pattern here reinforces the whole week's theme and is the right way to do animation: **CSS defines the animation; JavaScript (when needed) just toggles the class that triggers it.** The visual transition (fade and slide over 0.4s) lives entirely in CSS via `transition`, and JavaScript's only job is to add the `.visible` class at the right moment (when the element scrolls into view, detected with an `IntersectionObserver`). This is the same separation as the menu filter and dark mode, JS manages *when* (state, via classes), CSS handles *what it looks like*, and it matters because CSS animations are also *more performant* (the browser optimises them, often running them on the GPU) than animating with JavaScript directly. So the discipline holds: prefer CSS for the animation itself, use JavaScript only to trigger it by toggling a class. Much motion (hover effects, the smooth scroll, simple transitions) needs *no* JavaScript at all, pure CSS, which is simpler and faster, so reach for CSS-only first and add JS only when you need to trigger something on an event like scroll. ## The discipline of tasteful, accessible motion The most important lesson about animation is restraint and consideration, because motion is easy to overdo and can actively harm the experience: - **Subtle and purposeful:** good animation is barely noticed, it guides attention and adds smoothness (a gentle fade-in, a soft hover), where excessive animation (everything spinning, bouncing, sliding) is distracting, slow-feeling, and amateurish. The goal is *refinement*, not spectacle, less is almost always more. - **Fast:** animations should be quick (0.2-0.4s), a slow animation makes the site feel sluggish because the user is *waiting* for it; snappy motion feels responsive. - **Accessible:** some users get motion sickness or distraction from animation, and the web has a standard signal for this, `prefers-reduced-motion`, which you respect by disabling or reducing animations for users who have asked their system to minimise motion: ```css @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { * { transition: none; animation: none; } } ``` Honouring `prefers-reduced-motion` is a real accessibility responsibility, not optional, and respecting it shows the same user-consideration as semantic HTML and descriptive links. Tasteful, fast, accessible motion enhances a site; gratuitous, slow, motion-blind animation degrades it, and knowing the difference is a mark of a thoughtful frontend developer. ## Where this fits You added smooth scrolling and subtle, fast, accessible animations to Bean Forge, with CSS defining the motion and JavaScript only triggering it, and the discipline of restraint plus honouring `prefers-reduced-motion`. The site now feels refined. Tomorrow you ship Bean Forge v0.2, the interactive version.

items.body:
## Ship Bean Forge v0.2
You assemble the week's interactivity into a polished, shipped v0.2, a coffee shop site that now *responds*:
- a **daily special** that updates based on the day (data + logic + DOM).
- a **menu filter** driven by clicks (event listeners, class toggling, data attributes).
- **dark mode** that remembers the user's choice (localStorage persistence).
- smooth scrolling and **tasteful, accessible animation** (CSS motion, JS triggers, `prefers-reduced-motion`).
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Bean Forge v0.2: JavaScript interactivity (special, filter, dark mode, motion)"
git tag v0.2
git push origin main --tags
```
Pushing redeploys it on Netlify automatically (the W1 workflow), so v0.2 is live, and update the README's version log to record the new interactive features.

## What the interactivity week taught
Step back: you have learned how web pages come *alive*, and the patterns are remarkably consistent. Every feature this week, special, filter, dark mode, animation, was built from the same core: the **DOM** (find, change, listen), the **event-driven model** (register handlers, react to user actions), and the discipline of **JavaScript managing state by toggling CSS classes** while CSS handles the visuals. You also met persistence (localStorage), data attributes (data on elements for generic JS to act on), and the habits of polish (guarding edge cases, the dark-mode flash, accessible motion). These are not just techniques for a static site, they are the *exact* foundation that frameworks build on: React is, at heart, a much nicer way to do "when state changes, update the DOM," and understanding the raw version now means React will make sense as an *abstraction* rather than magic. The fundamentals you cemented, the DOM, events, state-via-classes, are what everything dynamic stands on.

## Where this fits
Bean Forge v0.2 is shipped and live: an interactive coffee shop site built on the DOM, events, and state-managed-via-classes, the raw foundation of all web interactivity. Next week you add a feature with real-world consequences, a contact form that actually delivers messages to an inbox (via Netlify Forms), teaching how forms work at the HTTP level, the model that underlies data submission across the entire web, and the bridge toward the backend work to come.

weeks.title: Bean Forge v0.3: Contact form with Netlify Forms
weeks.context:
A contact form that does not send email is a decoration. This week you wire Bean Forge's contact form to actually deliver messages to an inbox using Netlify Forms. When a stranger finds the coffee shop site and fills out the form, the owner gets an email. That is the feature. Building it requires understanding how forms work at the HTTP level, and understanding why the native form submission model, which predates JavaScript, still underlies most forms built today.

When a form's submit button is clicked, the browser packages up all the form field values and sends them to the URL specified in the form's action attribute using the method specified (GET or POST). For GET forms, the data is encoded in the URL query string. For POST forms, the data goes in the request body. The server receives the data and responds, typically with a redirect to a success page or with the same page plus an error message.

Netlify Forms hooks into this native browser behaviour. You add a netlify attribute to your form element and Netlify's CDN layer intercepts the POST request, stores the form submission in their dashboard, and sends you an email notification. No backend code required. No database. For a static site contact form, this is the correct solution, it is free, reliable, and requires zero infrastructure.

Form validation has two layers: client-side (JavaScript that runs in the browser before the form submits) and server-side (validation that happens after the data reaches the server). Client-side validation improves user experience, you can show "Please enter a valid email address" before the user submits, without a page reload. But client-side validation alone is insecure, a malicious user can bypass JavaScript entirely and submit arbitrary data. Always validate on the server too. For Netlify Forms, Netlify provides basic server-side validation (required fields) that you configure via the form's attributes.

Accessibility in forms is not optional. Every input must have an associated label (for screen readers). Error messages must be announced to screen readers (using aria-live). Keyboard navigation must work (users should be able to tab through the form and submit with Enter). These requirements are not edge cases, they affect millions of users who rely on assistive technology.

items.title: Why HTML forms
items.body:
## A form that does nothing is decoration
Bean Forge has a contact form, but right now it is *decoration*, fill it in, hit submit, and nothing happens. This week you make it real: when a stranger finds the coffee shop and fills out the form, the owner gets an **email**. That is the feature, and it is the first time Bean Forge does something that reaches the *real world* beyond the browser. You build it with **Netlify Forms** (which handles the email delivery for you), but the real learning is understanding *how forms work at the HTTP level*, because the native form-submission model, which predates JavaScript, still underlies essentially every form on the web, including the fanciest React ones.

## How a form actually submits
The foundational mechanism, worth understanding before any tool abstracts it: when a form's submit button is clicked, **the browser packages up all the form field values and sends them to a URL**, using the method you specify:
```html
<form action="/contact" method="POST">
  <input name="email" type="email">
  <textarea name="message"></textarea>
  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>
```
- The **`action`** is the URL the data is sent to.
- The **`method`** is how: **GET** (data encoded in the URL query string, for searches and safe, repeatable requests) or **POST** (data in the request body, for submitting/changing things, like a contact message).
- Each field's **`name`** is the key its value is sent under, so the server receives `email=...&message=...`.
The server receives the data and responds, typically by redirecting to a success page or re-showing the form with an error. This request/response cycle is the bedrock of how data gets from a browser to a server, and it has worked this way since before JavaScript existed.

## Why understanding native forms matters
It is tempting to skip straight to JavaScript-handled forms, but **understanding the native form model first is essential**, because it is what everything is built on and what saves you when things break. The native model, browser packages fields, sends them to a URL via GET/POST, server responds, is how the web has always submitted data, and even modern frameworks that intercept the submit with JavaScript are ultimately doing (or simulating) this same HTTP request underneath. Knowing the raw model gives you three things: you understand *what is actually being sent* (the field names and values, the method, the destination), which is exactly what you will work with when you build your own backends and APIs later (the POST request body, the form encoding); you can build forms that work *without* JavaScript (progressive enhancement, a form that still submits if JS fails, which is more robust and accessible); and you can debug form problems by reasoning about the HTTP request rather than treating the form as a mysterious black box. So this week, even using a convenient tool (Netlify Forms), you build on and understand the native mechanism, because that understanding is the durable foundation under every form you will ever build, from this contact form to a complex multi-step checkout.

## Where this fits
This week makes Bean Forge's contact form functional, delivering real emails via Netlify Forms, while teaching the native HTML form submission model (GET/POST, action, field names, the request/response cycle) that underlies all web data submission. It is the bridge from frontend-only work toward the backend, you are starting to send data to a server, which is what the Backend phase (W9-12) will have you handle yourself. Today's orientation: forms submit by the browser packaging fields and sending them to a URL via GET or POST, the bedrock model under every form, and you will make Bean Forge's form really deliver messages. Tomorrow you build the form properly.

items.title: Add the form
items.body:
## Build the form with the right inputs and structure
Today you build (or rebuild) Bean Forge's contact form properly, with the correct input types and a structure that is accessible and usable. The right HTML matters because the browser gives you a lot for free when you use it well:
```html
<form name="contact" method="POST" action="/success">
  <label for="name">Name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" type="text" required>

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <label for="message">Message</label>
  <textarea id="message" name="message" required></textarea>

  <button type="submit">Send message</button>
</form>
```
Each field has a `<label>` linked to it (via `for`/`id`), the right `type` (`email` for email, `tel` for phone, etc.), a `name` (the key the value is sent under), and `required` where appropriate.

## Labels and input types do real work
Two details here are not cosmetic, they provide real, free functionality, which is why using native form features well beats reinventing them:
- **Labels** (`<label for="email">`) are essential for **accessibility and usability**: a properly-linked label is announced by screen readers when the user focuses the field (so blind users know what to type), and it *expands the click target* (clicking the label focuses the input, easier on phones). A form with placeholder text instead of labels is a common, broken pattern, placeholders vanish when you type and are not reliably read by screen readers, so always use real labels.
- **Input types** give you correct behaviour for free: `type="email"` brings up the email keyboard on phones (with the @ key) and enables basic browser validation; `type="tel"` brings up the number pad; `type="password"` hides input. Using the right type means better mobile keyboards, appropriate validation, and clearer intent, all from one attribute.
Using native form semantics correctly, labels, types, `required`, is the same "use the platform's built-in features" discipline as semantic HTML, and it gives you accessibility, mobile-friendliness, and basic validation with almost no effort, where ignoring them means rebuilding all of that badly in JavaScript.

## Build forms for real humans
The deeper lesson is to build forms that are *easy and forgiving for real people to fill out*, because forms are where users do the work and where they get frustrated and abandon. Concretely: ask for the minimum (do not demand a phone number for a coffee-shop message), order fields logically, make labels clear, mark which fields are required, and use appropriate input types and reasonable field sizes. A contact form should feel effortless, a couple of clearly-labelled fields and a send button, not an interrogation. This user-centred mindset, the form serves the *person* filling it out, not the developer's convenience, is what makes the difference between forms people complete and forms they give up on, and it recurs everywhere forms appear (sign-ups, checkouts, settings). Building this contact form well, accessible labels, right input types, minimal friction, sets the standard for every form to come, and it is a place where small care (a linked label, the right keyboard on mobile) has an outsized effect on whether real users succeed.

## Where this fits
You built Bean Forge's contact form with proper structure, linked labels (for accessibility and bigger click targets), correct input types (for the right mobile keyboards and validation), and required fields, designed to be easy for real humans. Tomorrow you style it to match the site and to communicate clearly.

items.title: Style the form
items.body:
## Style the form to be clear and usable
A form needs styling that is not just attractive but *communicative*, it should make the fields obvious, show their state (focused, error, valid), and be comfortable to use. You style the inputs, labels, and button to match Bean Forge, with attention to the interactive states that guide the user:
```css
input, textarea {
  width: 100%; padding: 0.75rem; border: 1px solid #ccc; border-radius: 6px;
  font-size: 1rem;                           /* >=16px avoids iOS zoom-on-focus */
}
input:focus, textarea:focus {
  outline: 2px solid var(--coffee);          /* clear focus indicator */
  border-color: var(--coffee);
}
label { display: block; margin-bottom: 0.25rem; font-weight: 600; }
```
Generous padding, full-width fields, clear labels, and an obvious **focus state** (showing which field is active) make the form easy to use.

## State styling guides the user
The most important form-styling idea beyond looks is **styling the states**, because a form communicates through its visual feedback, and good state styling is what makes a form feel responsive and clear:
- **Focus state:** the currently-active field should be visually distinct (a coloured outline/border), so the user always knows where their typing will go, this is *especially* important for keyboard users who tab between fields, and removing the focus outline (a common mistake done for "looks") is a serious accessibility failure. Style focus to be clear and on-brand, never remove it.
- **Error and valid states:** when validation runs (next, D5 spam and beyond), invalid fields should look invalid (red border, an error message) and the message should say *what* to fix, so the user can correct it, an error state with no explanation is frustrating.
- **The submit button** should look clickable, and ideally show a "sending..." state on submit so the user knows something is happening.
These states turn a form from a static set of boxes into something that *responds* and *guides*, which is what makes filling it out feel smooth rather than uncertain. One mobile-specific detail above: font-size of at least 16px on inputs prevents iOS from auto-zooming when a field is focused (a jarring, common mobile annoyance), a small fix that shows attention to the real mobile experience.

## Clarity over decoration
The guiding principle for form styling is **clarity over decoration**: a form's job is to be easy to complete, so styling should *aid* that (clear fields, obvious focus, readable labels, visible errors), not get in the way (low-contrast text, fields that do not look like fields, hidden labels, decorative flourishes that confuse). This is a specific case of the broader truth that good design serves the user's task, a contact form that looks stunning but is confusing to fill out is a worse form than a plain one that is crystal clear. So you style for *usability first*: make it obvious what to type where, show state clearly, ensure good contrast and tap-friendly sizes, and let it look good *in service of* being easy. This discipline, function and clarity first, decoration in support, is exactly the design judgement that the Tailwind and design-systems week (W7) will deepen, and forms are an excellent place to practise it because their entire purpose is user input, so any styling that hampers input is straightforwardly wrong. A clear, well-stated form is a form people complete.

## Where this fits
You styled Bean Forge's form for clarity and usability: comfortable fields, clear labels, an obvious focus state (never removed), readable on mobile (16px+ to avoid zoom), with state styling that guides the user, prioritising clarity over decoration. Tomorrow you connect it to Netlify Forms so it actually delivers messages.

items.title: Push to Netlify and enable Forms
items.body:
## Make it deliver: Netlify Forms
Now the form becomes *functional*. **Netlify Forms** delivers submissions to the site owner with almost no code, you mark the form so Netlify detects it, and Netlify handles capturing the submission and emailing it. The magic is one attribute:
```html
<form name="contact" method="POST" data-netlify="true">
  ...fields with name attributes...
</form>
```
When you deploy to Netlify (the W1 GitHub-push workflow), Netlify scans your HTML at build time, finds forms marked `data-netlify="true"`, and automatically wires them up: submissions are captured, stored in your Netlify dashboard, and (once you configure a notification) emailed to the owner. So a stranger fills out the form, hits send, and the coffee shop owner gets an email, the feature, working, with no server code from you.

## What Netlify is doing for you (and what that teaches)
It is worth understanding *what* Netlify Forms handles, because it makes concrete the backend work you will later do yourself, and using it thoughtfully (not just magically) teaches the shape of the problem. Submitting a form to "an inbox" actually requires several things: a **server** to receive the POST request, somewhere to **store** the submission, and a way to **send an email** notification, and Netlify provides all three so you do not have to (yet). This is a perfect example of using a managed service to ship a real feature now while you are still learning, the same build-vs-buy judgement from across the tracks, you get a working contact form today, and you will learn to build the receiving server, the storage, and the email-sending yourself in the Backend (W9-12) and Email (W14) phases. So Netlify Forms is both a practical tool *and* a preview: it shows you the *pieces* of handling a form submission (receive, store, notify) by handling them for you, so that when you build those pieces yourself later, you know what they are *for*. Reach for the managed solution to ship, and understand what it is abstracting so you can build it when you need to.

## Verify it actually works
The essential discipline whenever you wire up something that crosses to the real world (sending an email, charging a card, saving data) is to **verify it end-to-end**, do not assume it works because the code looks right. Deploy the form, then *actually submit it* and confirm: does the submission appear in the Netlify dashboard? Does the notification email arrive in the inbox? Does the data come through correctly (all fields, readable)? This real test catches the things that "looks correct" misses, a missing `name` attribute (so a field's value never arrives), a form not detected (a deploy/config issue), the notification email not configured (submissions captured but no email sent), or the email landing in spam. Testing the *real* behaviour of a real-world integration is non-negotiable, because the whole value of the feature is that it works in reality, a contact form that silently fails to deliver is worse than no form, since the owner misses messages without knowing. So you submit a test message, watch it arrive, and only then trust it. This habit, verify the real-world effect, not just the code, becomes critical for the higher-stakes integrations ahead (payments, especially), and the contact form is a low-stakes place to build it.

## Where this fits
Bean Forge's form now delivers real emails via Netlify Forms (the `data-netlify` attribute, wired up automatically on deploy), and you understand that Netlify is handling the receive-store-notify pieces you will later build yourself, verified by actually submitting and confirming the email arrives. Tomorrow you protect it from the spam that every public form attracts.

items.title: Spam protection
items.body:
## Every public form attracts spam A contact form open to the internet *will* get spam, automated bots submit junk to public forms constantly, and an owner buried in spam misses the real messages. **Spam protection** is therefore a required part of any real form, not an optional extra. Netlify provides built-in protection, and the classic technique it uses is the **honeypot**: a hidden field that humans never see (and so leave empty) but bots, which fill in every field they find, *do* fill, so a non-empty honeypot field flags a submission as spam: ```html

...real fields...
``` The `bot-field` is hidden from real users via CSS/`hidden`; if it arrives filled, a bot did it, and the submission is rejected. ## Why honeypots are elegant, and what else exists The honeypot is worth understanding because it is a clever, low-friction approach and it illustrates the spam-fighting trade-off: - **Honeypot** (the field bots fill but humans do not): invisible to real users, so it adds *zero friction* for legitimate visitors, no puzzle, no clicking, while catching the dumb bots that fill every field. Its limit is that sophisticated bots can learn to skip hidden fields, so it stops a lot but not everything. - **CAPTCHA** (reCAPTCHA, "select all the traffic lights," or the invisible/checkbox versions): more effective against advanced bots, but it adds *friction* for real users (annoying puzzles, accessibility problems for some users), so it is a heavier tool you reach for when honeypots are not enough. - **Rate limiting** (server-side, later): blocking too many submissions from one source. The trade-off is **effectiveness versus user friction**: the honeypot is friction-free but beatable, CAPTCHA is stronger but irritating, so you use the lightest protection that works (honeypot first, CAPTCHA only if spam remains a problem), to avoid taxing real users more than necessary. This "protect against abuse with the least burden on legitimate users" judgement recurs throughout security (W21) and is a good principle: do not make all your real users solve puzzles to stop bots a honeypot would catch. ## Spam protection as part of building responsibly The broader lesson is that **building a feature for the real world means anticipating its abuse**, and a public form is your first encounter with that. The naive view is "I built a contact form, done"; the real-world view is "I built a public endpoint that bots will target, so I must protect it." This mindset, every public-facing thing will be probed and abused, so design for that from the start, is foundational to building production software, and it scales up dramatically (the Security week, W21, is entirely about the threats you have not thought about). Adding spam protection to the contact form is a low-stakes, concrete first lesson in it: you are not just making the form *work*, you are making it *survive contact with the open internet*, where automated abuse is constant. Internalising that "public-facing" implies "will be abused," and building the appropriate (least-friction) protection in from the start, is the responsible-engineering habit that the contact form introduces and that everything production-facing later demands. A feature is not done when it works for good actors; it is done when it also withstands the bad ones. ## Where this fits You protected Bean Forge's form from spam with a honeypot (friction-free for real users, catches naive bots), understanding the effectiveness-vs-friction trade-off (honeypot, CAPTCHA, rate limiting) and the deeper habit that public-facing features must anticipate abuse. Tomorrow you complete the experience with a proper success page.

items.title: Success page
items.body:
## Close the loop: the success page
When a user submits the form, they need clear confirmation that it worked, leaving them on the same form, or showing nothing, is confusing and makes people resubmit or assume failure. A **success page** closes the loop: after submission, the user is taken to (or shown) a clear "Thanks, we got your message" confirmation. With Netlify Forms, you point the form's `action` to a success page, or use Netlify's redirect:
```html
<form name="contact" method="POST" data-netlify="true" action="/thanks/">
```
Then `/thanks/` is a real page that confirms success warmly: "Thanks for reaching out, Bean Forge will get back to you soon," ideally with a link back to the site. The user *knows* their message went through, and the experience feels complete rather than uncertain.

## Feedback is part of the feature
The principle here is that **a feature is not complete until the user knows the outcome**, feedback is part of the feature, not an afterthought. A form that submits successfully but gives no confirmation is, from the user's perspective, *broken*, because they cannot tell if it worked, so they worry, resubmit (sending duplicate messages), or give up. The success page provides the *closure* that makes the interaction trustworthy: action taken, clear confirmation, user reassured. This generalises far beyond forms, every action a user takes (clicking a button, saving a setting, making a payment) needs clear feedback about its result (success, failure, in-progress), and designing that feedback is core to good UX. The contact form teaches it concretely: the message sending is only half the feature; *telling the user it sent* is the other half. Thinking about the *whole* interaction, including the confirmation, the error case, the loading state, rather than just the happy-path mechanics, is what makes features feel finished and reliable.

## Handle the unhappy path too
A complete feature also considers what happens when things *do not* go well, the unhappy path, because real submissions sometimes fail (network error, server hiccup, validation problem). Good feedback covers all outcomes:
- **Success:** the confirmation page/message (done above).
- **Error:** if submission fails, the user should see a clear, non-technical message ("Something went wrong, please try again or email us directly") rather than a silent failure or a cryptic error, so they know to retry and are not left stranded.
- **In-progress:** for slower submissions, a "sending..." state on the button (disabling it to prevent double-submits) tells the user it is working and stops duplicate sends.
You do not need elaborate handling for a simple Netlify form, but *thinking about the unhappy path*, what if it fails? what does the user see and do then?, is the discipline that distinguishes robust features from fragile ones. The beginner codes only the success case; the careful developer asks "and if it fails?" and makes that case graceful too. Closing the loop fully, success, error, and progress all clearly communicated, is what makes a feature genuinely trustworthy for real users, and the contact form is a clean place to practise covering all three.

## Where this fits
You closed the loop with a success page that clearly confirms the submission worked, internalising that feedback is part of the feature (a result the user cannot see is a feature that feels broken) and that the unhappy path (error and in-progress states) needs handling too. Tomorrow you tag v0.3, the fully-functional contact form.

items.body:
## Ship Bean Forge v0.3
You assemble the week into v0.3, a contact form that genuinely works, end to end:
- a well-built form (proper inputs, linked labels, right types, required fields) styled for clarity with clear focus and state styling.
- real email delivery via **Netlify Forms** (verified by an actual test submission arriving in the inbox).
- **spam protection** (a friction-free honeypot) because it is a public endpoint.
- a **success page** closing the loop, with awareness of the error and in-progress cases.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Bean Forge v0.3: working contact form with Netlify Forms, spam protection, success page"
git tag v0.3
git push origin main --tags
```

## What the form week taught
Step back: Bean Forge now does something real, it connects a website visitor to the shop owner via email, and building it taught the foundations of *data submission*, which is much of what web applications do. You learned the native HTML form model (GET/POST, action, field names, the request/response cycle) that underlies all form submission and previews the backends you will build; you learned to build forms for real humans (accessible labels, right input types, minimal friction); you used a managed service (Netlify) to ship a real feature while understanding the receive-store-notify pieces it abstracts; and you built the real-world disciplines of anticipating abuse (spam protection), verifying end-to-end (a test submission), and closing the loop (success, error, progress feedback). These are not coffee-shop-specific, they are the foundations of every form and data submission on the web, from this contact form to a checkout to a complex application form, and the native-model understanding especially is the durable knowledge under all of it.

## Where this fits
Bean Forge v0.3 is shipped: a real, working, spam-protected contact form that delivers email and confirms success, teaching the foundations of web data submission. Next week you tackle the problem that plain HTML files create as a site grows, *duplication* (the same nav copied into every page), by refactoring Bean Forge to the **Astro** framework, your first taste of components, templates, and build tools, which solve the "20 pages, one change" problem and bridge you toward the component-based frontend work (React, Next.js) ahead.

weeks.title: Bean Forge v0.4: Refactor to Astro + add /blog
weeks.context:
Plain HTML files work. They are fast, simple, and require no tooling. They also do not scale when you have 20 pages with the same navigation header that needs updating. Copy-pasting the same navigation code into 20 HTML files means 20 files to update when the navigation changes. This is the problem that components, templates, and build tools solve. Astro is the framework that lets you have the best of both worlds: the simplicity of static HTML at runtime, with the component model during development.

Astro components compile to HTML. A Menu.astro component that accepts props (item data) renders to plain HTML when built, no JavaScript framework in the browser, no React runtime, no Vue runtime. Just the HTML the browser needs. This makes Astro sites fast by default: there is nothing extra to download or execute. JavaScript is added only when you explicitly need interactivity, using Astro's "islands" architecture.

The refactor from plain HTML to Astro teaches you what a framework actually does. You are not abandoning the fundamentals, you are adding a build step that lets you write more maintainable code that compiles to the same thing you were writing manually. Understanding what compiles to what is how you debug build tools rather than just hoping they work.

Adding a /blog to Bean Forge introduces markdown. Markdown is plain text with simple formatting conventions: # for headings, ** for bold, * for italics, [text](url) for links. Astro processes .md files and converts them to HTML automatically. This is the architecture behind most modern content sites: developers write in markdown, the build tool converts to HTML, the result is fast and accessible.

The build step introduces a new failure mode: your site works locally but breaks after building. Local development runs a dev server that serves files directly. The build process transforms and optimises files in ways that can expose issues, wrong import paths, missing dependencies, environment variables that exist locally but not in the build environment. Testing the built output (npm run build && npm run preview) before deploying is a habit worth developing.

items.title: What is Astro?
items.body:
## The problem plain HTML creates as it grows
Plain HTML files are great, fast, simple, no tooling, and you built three versions of Bean Forge with them. But they do not *scale*: imagine Bean Forge grows to 20 pages, all sharing the same navigation header. Change the nav (add a link, fix the logo), and you must edit *20 files* identically, and miss one and the site is inconsistent. This **duplication** problem, the same code copy-pasted across many files, all needing to change together, is exactly what components, templates, and build tools solve. This week you refactor Bean Forge to **Astro**, a framework that gives you the best of both worlds: a *component model* during development (write the nav once, use it everywhere) that compiles down to *plain fast HTML* at runtime.

## What Astro is and why it fits here
**Astro** is a web framework built around a simple, powerful idea: **components that compile to HTML**. You write a `Nav.astro` component once, use it on every page, and when Astro *builds* the site, it renders everything to plain HTML, no React runtime, no framework JavaScript shipped to the browser, just the HTML the browser needs. This makes Astro sites **fast by default**: there is nothing extra to download or execute, unlike heavier frameworks that ship a JavaScript runtime. JavaScript is added *only* where you explicitly need interactivity. This is the perfect bridge for you right now: you keep the speed and simplicity of the static HTML you understand, while gaining the *component model* (reusable pieces, no duplication) that all modern frontend development uses, and that React and Next.js (the next phase) are built on. Astro lets you learn components without yet taking on a full JavaScript framework's complexity.

## What you'll do this week
This week's work is a **refactor**, taking the working Bean Forge and rebuilding it on Astro *without changing what users see*, plus adding a blog:
- set up Astro and understand its component model.
- **port** the existing Bean Forge pages into Astro.
- **extract** the repeated pieces (nav, footer, menu items) into reusable components, eliminating the duplication.
- add a **/blog** with multiple posts, which is exactly where the components-and-templates payoff shows (many pages sharing one layout).
A refactor, improving the *structure* of working code without changing its behaviour, is itself an important skill, and doing it here teaches both Astro and the discipline of restructuring code safely.

## Where this fits
This week completes the Foundations phase by introducing the *component model* via Astro, solving the duplication problem of plain HTML and bridging toward the component-based frontend frameworks (React in W5, Next.js in W6) that the rest of the track uses. It is the step from "hand-written HTML pages" to "composed, reusable components," the mental shift that underlies all modern frontend. Today's orientation: plain HTML does not scale because of duplication, and Astro solves it with components that compile to fast plain HTML, giving the component model without a heavy runtime. Tomorrow you set up Astro.

items.title: Set up Astro
items.body:
## Set up Astro and meet a build tool
Today you set up an Astro project, which is also your first real encounter with a **build tool** and a Node-based development workflow, the standard modern setup you will use for every framework ahead:
```bash
npm create astro@latest bean-forge-astro    # scaffold a new Astro project
cd bean-forge-astro
npm install                                  # install dependencies
npm run dev                                  # start the local dev server (live reload)
```
`npm` (Node's package manager) installs the project's dependencies, `npm run dev` starts a **development server** that serves your site locally and *auto-reloads* the browser when you save a change (a huge upgrade from manually refreshing), and later `npm run build` compiles everything to static files for deployment. This npm-install-dev-build workflow is the bedrock of modern web development, you will use it in every project from here on.

## Understanding the moving parts
A few concepts from this setup are worth grounding, because they recur everywhere and confuse beginners when left mysterious:
- **`package.json`** is the project's manifest: it lists your dependencies (the libraries the project uses) and defines the `scripts` (`dev`, `build`) you run with `npm run`. It is the project's identity card.
- **`node_modules`** is where npm installs all those dependencies (it gets large, and it is git-ignored, you commit `package.json`, not `node_modules`, and anyone can regenerate the modules with `npm install`).
- **The dev server vs the build:** `npm run dev` runs a live development server (fast feedback, auto-reload) for *while you work*; `npm run build` produces the optimised static output for *deployment*. Development and production are different modes, a distinction that matters increasingly as projects grow.
Understanding these, the manifest, where dependencies live, the dev-vs-build distinction, demystifies the modern toolchain, which otherwise feels like a pile of magic config. You do not need to master build tools now, but knowing *what* `package.json`, `node_modules`, and the dev/build scripts are makes the whole workflow legible rather than intimidating.

## The shift from files to a project
The deeper change here is conceptual: you are moving from *loose HTML files you open directly* to a *project with tooling that builds your site*, and this is the shape of all modern web development, so embracing it now matters. With plain HTML, the file you wrote *is* the file the browser runs; with a build tool, you write *source* (components, templates) and the tool *compiles* it into the HTML/CSS/JS that ships. This indirection buys you enormous power (components, reuse, optimisation, modern syntax) at the cost of a build step and some tooling to understand, and that trade, a bit more setup for a lot more capability, defines modern frontend. The reason to make this shift on Astro specifically is that Astro's output is *still just HTML* (so the result is close to what you already understand), making it a gentle on-ramp to the build-tool world before you reach heavier frameworks. Getting comfortable with "I write source, a tool builds the site, a dev server shows it live" is the foundational workflow mindset for everything ahead, and Astro is the ideal place to acquire it because the gap between your source and the output stays small and comprehensible.

## Where this fits
You set up an Astro project and met the modern toolchain: npm for dependencies, `package.json` as the manifest, `node_modules` for installed libraries, a dev server with live reload, and the build step, the npm-install-dev-build workflow you will use everywhere. You have made the shift from loose files to a built project. Tomorrow you port Bean Forge's pages into Astro.

items.title: Port Bean Forge to Astro
items.body:
## Port Bean Forge into Astro Today you move the existing Bean Forge into Astro, which starts gently because **Astro components are mostly just HTML**. An Astro page (`.astro` file) has an optional script section (between `---` fences, for logic) and then markup that is essentially HTML: ```astro --- // component script (runs at build time): imports, data, props const shopName = "Bean Forge"; --- {shopName}

{shopName}

Welcome to our coffee shop.

``` You create pages in `src/pages/` (Astro uses **file-based routing**, `src/pages/about.astro` becomes the `/about` URL automatically), and you paste your existing HTML in, then sprinkle in dynamic bits with `{ }` (which embeds JavaScript values, like `{shopName}`). Most of your HTML works as-is, which is the point: Astro is HTML *plus* superpowers, not a replacement. ## File-based routing and embedded expressions Two Astro mechanics from this port are worth understanding because they are powerful and recur in Next.js later: - **File-based routing:** the *files in `src/pages/`* define your URLs. `index.astro` is `/`, `about.astro` is `/about`, `blog/first-post.astro` is `/blog/first-post`. There is no separate routing configuration, the file structure *is* the route structure, which is intuitive and is exactly how Next.js's routing works too (W6), so learning it here transfers directly. - **Embedded expressions (`{ }`):** inside the markup, `{ }` lets you drop in JavaScript values and expressions, `{shopName}`, `{new Date().getFullYear()}` for a dynamic copyright year, `{menu.map(item =>
  • {item}
    • )}` to render a list. This blends static HTML with dynamic data cleanly, and it is the same JSX-like `{ }` syntax React uses, so again, you are learning a transferable pattern. Porting the pages teaches these by doing, and because the gap from your hand-written HTML to Astro is small (file = route, HTML + `{ }`), the port is a confidence-building bridge rather than a leap. ## Refactor safely: behaviour first, structure second The discipline this day teaches is **safe refactoring**: you are restructuring working code (moving Bean Forge to Astro) *without changing what the user sees*, and doing that safely has a method. Port incrementally, get one page working in Astro and verify it looks identical to the original, *then* the next, rather than rewriting everything at once and hoping. Keep the original as a reference to compare against. After each step, run the dev server and check the result matches the old site, because the goal of *this* refactor is behavioural sameness (the user should not notice), so any visible difference means you broke something in the move. This "change the structure, preserve the behaviour, verify continuously" approach is the essence of refactoring, and it is a critical professional skill, because much real work is improving existing code (making it cleaner, faster, more maintainable) *without* breaking what works, and doing that safely (incrementally, with constant verification) is what lets you improve a codebase confidently rather than fearfully. The Bean Forge port is a clean place to practise it: you have a known-good target (the existing site), so you can verify the refactor preserved it exactly. ## Where this fits You ported Bean Forge into Astro, learning that Astro components are HTML plus `{ }` expressions, that file-based routing maps files to URLs (transferable to Next.js), and the safe-refactor discipline of restructuring incrementally while verifying the behaviour is preserved. The site now runs on Astro but looks the same. Tomorrow you get the real payoff: extracting reusable components to kill the duplication.

items.title: Component extraction
items.body:
## The payoff: extract reusable components Now you solve the problem that motivated the whole week, **duplication**, by extracting the repeated pieces into reusable **components**. The nav, footer, and menu-item markup that would otherwise be copied across pages each become a single component, written once and used everywhere: ```astro --- // src/components/Nav.astro ---
Home Menu Blog
``` ```astro --- // any page: import Nav from '../components/Nav.astro'; ---
``` Now the navigation is defined in *one place*, and every page that uses `
` gets it. Change the nav once, and it updates everywhere, the "20 pages, one change" problem, solved. ## Props make components flexible Components become truly powerful with **props**, inputs that let one component render differently in different places, so you write the *structure* once and pass in the *data*. A `MenuItem` component takes the item's details as props: ```astro --- // src/components/MenuItem.astro const { name, price, description } = Astro.props; // receive props ---

{name}

{description}

${price}
``` ```astro ``` One `MenuItem` definition, used for every drink, with the specifics passed as props. This is the heart of the component model: a component is a *reusable template* that takes props and renders accordingly, so you describe a menu item's structure *once* and reuse it for all items. Combined with looping (`menu.map(item => )`), you render an entire menu from data with one component, exactly the data-driven rendering you glimpsed with the daily special, now properly structured. ## Why components are the foundation of modern frontend The deeper significance is that **components are the fundamental building block of all modern frontend development**, and extracting them here teaches the mental model that React, Next.js, Vue, everything uses. The core idea, *break the UI into reusable, composable pieces, each with a clear job, parameterised by props*, is universal: - **Reuse, no duplication:** define once, use everywhere, the immediate win (one nav, one footer, one menu-item template). - **Maintainability:** a change to a component updates every use, and a bug fixed once is fixed everywhere, so the codebase stays consistent and easy to change. - **Composability:** pages are *built from* components (a page is a `Header` + `Hero` + `Menu` + `Footer`), and components can contain other components, so complex UIs are assembled from simple, understandable pieces, like building with blocks. - **Reasoning:** you understand and test one component in isolation, then trust it everywhere it is used. This component thinking, decompose the UI into reusable parametrised pieces and compose them, is *the* paradigm of modern frontend, and Astro teaches it cleanly (with components that are just HTML + props), so that when you reach React next week, components will be a *familiar* idea expressed in new syntax, not a new concept. Learning to *see* a UI as a composition of components is one of the most important frontend skills, and the Bean Forge refactor is where you start. ## Where this fits You extracted Bean Forge's repeated markup into reusable components (Nav, Footer, MenuItem) with props for flexibility, killing the duplication and learning the component model, decompose the UI into reusable, parametrised, composable pieces, that is the foundation of all modern frontend and transfers directly to React. Tomorrow you add a /blog, where the component-and-layout payoff really shows.
