items.title: Add a /blog page
items.body:
## Add a /blog: where templates shine A blog is the perfect feature to show off components and templates, because every blog post shares the *same layout* (header, post title, content area, footer) with *different content*, exactly the reuse components are for. You build a blog where one **layout** wraps every post: ```astro --- // src/layouts/BlogPost.astro -- the shared shell for every post const { title, date } = Astro.props; --- {title}

{title}

{date}
``` The `` is where each post's unique content is inserted, so the layout provides the *consistent shell* and each post provides only its *content*. Add a post by writing its content and wrapping it in the layout, no header/footer/structure repetition. ## Layouts, slots, and content collections This blog introduces a few patterns that are central to content-driven sites: - **Layouts:** a layout is a component that defines the shared *page shell* (the parts every page of a type has in common) with a `` for the page-specific content. This is the ultimate anti-duplication tool, one `BlogPost` layout means every post automatically has the right header, footer, and structure, and a change to the layout updates *all* posts. (The same idea gives you a `BaseLayout` for the whole site.) - **Slots:** `` is the "insert the content here" placeholder that makes layouts work, the wrapping component provides the frame, the wrapped content fills the slot. - **Markdown content:** Astro lets you write blog posts in **Markdown** (`.md` files, simple text with light formatting), and render them through a layout, so writing a post is writing prose, not HTML, and Astro's *content collections* organise many such posts. This is how content-heavy sites (blogs, docs) are efficiently built: content in Markdown, presentation in a layout. Together, layouts + slots + Markdown make adding the tenth blog post as easy as the first, because all the *structure* is shared and only the *content* differs. ## The principle: separate content from presentation, at scale The blog crystallises a principle that has run through the whole foundations phase and scales up here: **separate the content from its presentation, and define the presentation once.** With plain HTML, each blog post would repeat the entire page structure (duplication, the week's villain); with layouts and slots, the *presentation* (the post shell) is defined once and *every* post reuses it, while the *content* (each post's text) is separate and minimal. This is the same content-vs-presentation separation as HTML-vs-CSS from week one, now at the page level: the layout is the reusable presentation, the Markdown posts are the content, and they combine at build time. The payoff is exactly what a growing site needs, you can add many pages cheaply (just content) and restyle them all at once (just the layout), which is precisely the scalability plain HTML lacked. This pattern, shared layouts wrapping individual content, is how essentially every real content site is built (and Next.js has the same layout concept), so learning it on Bean Forge's blog teaches a directly transferable, fundamental approach to structuring multi-page sites. The blog is small, but it demonstrates the architecture that lets a site grow to hundreds of pages without the duplication nightmare. ## Where this fits You added a /blog using a shared layout with a `` for content and Markdown for the posts, demonstrating layouts, slots, and content/presentation separation at scale, the architecture (define presentation once, add content cheaply) that lets sites grow without duplication, and that transfers to Next.js. Tomorrow you build and deploy the Astro site.

items.title: Build + deploy on Netlify
items.body:
## Build and deploy the Astro site
Astro sites need a **build step** before deployment (unlike plain HTML), so today you build and deploy, learning how a framework site goes from source to live. Locally, `npm run build` compiles your components, layouts, and Markdown into a folder of optimised static HTML/CSS/JS:
```bash
npm run build       # compiles src/ into dist/ (plain static files)
npm run preview     # preview the production build locally
```
Then deployment is the familiar GitHub-to-Netlify flow, except now Netlify runs the *build command* for you: you configure Netlify to run `npm run build` and publish the `dist/` output, push to GitHub, and Netlify installs dependencies, builds the site, and serves the result.
```text
push to GitHub -> Netlify: npm install -> npm run build -> publish dist/ -> live
```

## The build step, and why the output is still fast
This introduces the crucial idea that **a framework site is *compiled* before it is served**, and understanding the build makes deployment legible rather than mysterious. Your *source* (`.astro` components, layouts, Markdown) is not what the browser runs, the build *transforms* it into plain static HTML/CSS (and minimal JS), and *that* output is what gets deployed and served. This is why Astro sites are fast despite the component model: all the component composition, the layouts, the Markdown rendering happens *at build time*, on the server, producing plain HTML, so the *browser* receives just fast static files with no framework runtime, you get the developer-experience benefits of components and the runtime performance of static HTML, because the heavy lifting is done at build time, not in the user's browser. This build-time-vs-runtime distinction is fundamental to modern web frameworks (and central to Next.js's rendering strategies in W6), so grasping it here, "I write components, the build compiles them to static HTML, the browser gets the fast result", is foundational. The Netlify deploy now running your build command is also your first taste of a deployment pipeline doing real work (install, build, publish), which scales up to the full CI/CD of W19.

## Verify the deployed build
The discipline, as always with anything that goes live, is to **verify the deployed result**, especially now that a build sits between your source and the live site, because the build can behave differently from your local dev server. After deploying, check the live Astro site: does it look and work identically to local? Did the build succeed (check Netlify's build log if not)? Common build-time surprises to watch for, a path that worked locally but is wrong in production, an import that the build cannot resolve, an environment difference, all of which show up only when you actually build and deploy, not in the dev server. This is the framework-era version of the W1 "verify it's live" habit, now with a build step that adds its own potential failure points, so verifying the *built and deployed* site (not just `npm run dev`) is essential. The build introduces the classic "works in dev, breaks in build" class of issues, and the only way to catch them is to actually run the build and check the deployed output, which is exactly why you verify rather than assume. A green local dev server does not guarantee a working production build, so you confirm the real thing.

## Where this fits
You built and deployed the Astro Bean Forge: `npm run build` compiles your components and Markdown to fast static HTML, Netlify runs the build on push and serves the output, and you verified the deployed build matches local. You understand the build-time-vs-runtime distinction (compile components to static HTML, browser gets the fast result) that underlies modern frameworks. Tomorrow you tag v0.4 and add a second blog post, completing the foundations phase.

items.title: Tag v0.4 + write a 2nd blog post
items.body:
## Ship Bean Forge v0.4 and complete the foundations
You finish the refactor and ship v0.4, Bean Forge rebuilt on a component model:
- **Astro** with reusable components (Nav, Footer, MenuItem with props) eliminating duplication.
- a **/blog** using a shared layout, slots, and Markdown, with a *second* blog post added (proving the template pays off, the second post is nearly free).
- built and deployed via Netlify's build pipeline, verified live.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Bean Forge v0.4: refactored to Astro with components, layouts, and a blog"
git tag v0.4
git push origin main --tags
```
Writing that second blog post is the proof of the week: it takes minutes, because the layout, nav, and footer are all reused, you write only the content, which is exactly the scalability the refactor bought.

## What the foundations phase delivered
Step back across four weeks: you took Bean Forge from a single hand-written HTML page to a component-based, content-driven, framework-built site, and along the way you learned the *complete foundation* of web development from first principles. You understand what a website fundamentally is (files over HTTP), the three languages and their separation (HTML structure, CSS style, JS behaviour), how interactivity works (the DOM, events, state via classes), how data submission works (the native form model), and how modern development is structured (build tools, components, layouts, the npm workflow). Crucially, you learned these *from the ground up*, raw HTML before Astro, the DOM before any framework, so you understand what the tools *do for you*. This is the deliberate payoff of starting with fundamentals: when you reach React next week, components, props, and `{ }` expressions will be *familiar concepts* in new syntax, not magic, because you built the un-abstracted version yourself. You also built real habits throughout, semantic HTML, accessibility, responsive design, shipping early, polish, verifying the real result, that carry through everything ahead.

## Where this fits
Bean Forge v0.4 is shipped, a component-based Astro site with a blog, completing the Foundations phase. You command web development from first principles, files, the three languages, interactivity, forms, and the component model, with the un-abstracted understanding that makes frameworks legible. Next comes the **Frontend phase** (W5-8): **React**, the component-based library behind most of the modern web, where the component thinking you just learned in Astro becomes a powerful, interactive, industry-standard tool, followed by Next.js, Tailwind, and state management, the frontend stack most jobs actually use.

weeks.title: React, The Component Mental Model
weeks.context:
React is the component mental model. Every UI you will build in your career will be decomposed into components, self-contained units that manage their own state and render a piece of the interface. React invented this mental model (or popularised it, it is a contested history) and most modern UI frameworks use a variation of it. Learning React means learning how to think about interfaces as trees of components, which is a transferable skill regardless of which framework you use next.

A component is a function that takes data (props) as input and returns a description of what to display (JSX). React calls your function, takes the JSX you returned, and updates the DOM to match. When the props or state change, React calls your function again and updates only the parts of the DOM that changed. This is fundamentally different from the imperative DOM manipulation you learned in weeks 1-2 (document.querySelector().textContent = ...), you describe what the UI should look like given the current data, and React handles the how.

useState is the hook that gives function components the ability to remember values between renders. When you call useState(initialValue), you get back the current value and a setter function. Calling the setter function triggers a re-render with the new value. This is the fundamental React loop: user action triggers a state change, state change triggers a re-render, re-render produces updated UI.

The rules of hooks are not arbitrary. Hooks must be called at the top level of the component function, not inside conditions or loops. This constraint exists because React relies on the order of hook calls to associate state with the right component instance across renders. Violating the rules produces subtle bugs where state gets mixed up between renders.

The expense tracker beyond expenses is more than an exercise, it is a template for state-driven UI. The same pattern applies to a shopping cart, a form builder, a kanban board, or a dashboard. Data flows down (through props), events bubble up (through callback props). Once you internalise this one-directional data flow, every React application you build makes sense.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## React is the component mental model
You learned components in Astro; **React** makes them *interactive* and is the industry standard, the library most of the modern web's interfaces are built with. But the deepest thing React teaches is not its API, it is a *way of thinking*: every UI you build in your career will be **decomposed into components**, self-contained units that manage their own state and render a piece of the interface, and you compose those components into a *tree* that is your whole UI. React invented (or popularised) this mental model, and nearly every modern UI framework now uses a variation of it, so learning to *think in components and trees* is a transferable skill regardless of which framework you use next. This week you learn React by building interactive components, and in doing so internalise the component mental model that underlies all modern frontend.

## The fundamental shift: declarative, not imperative
React works fundamentally differently from the DOM manipulation you did in weeks 1-2, and grasping this shift is the key to everything. Back then you were **imperative**: you found elements and *told the browser exactly what to change* (`element.textContent = ...`, `element.classList.add(...)`), step by step. React is **declarative**: a component is a function that takes data (**props**) and returns a *description* of what the UI should look like (**JSX**), and React figures out how to update the DOM to match.
```text
imperative (weeks 1-2):  "find this element, change its text, add this class" (you do the steps)
declarative (React):     "given this data, the UI looks like THIS" (React does the DOM updates)
```
You describe the *what* (the UI as a function of the data), and React handles the *how* (the DOM changes). When the data changes, React calls your function again and updates *only the parts of the DOM that actually changed*. This is a profound simplification: instead of manually keeping the DOM in sync with your data as it changes (error-prone, the source of countless bugs), you just describe the UI for any given data, and React keeps the DOM in sync for you.

## Why declarative wins
Understanding *why* the declarative model is better explains why React took over. In the imperative world, as an app grows, you have data changing and you must remember to manually update *every* part of the DOM that depends on it, every place the data is shown, on every change, and miss one and the UI is out of sync with the data (a classic bug: the count updates here but not there). The declarative model eliminates this entire class of bugs: you write the UI as a function of the data *once*, and React guarantees the DOM always reflects the current data by re-running your function and updating what changed whenever the data updates. So you stop thinking "what DOM operations do I need to perform to get from the old state to the new state?" (hard, bug-prone) and start thinking "what should the UI look like for this state?" (simple, declarative). This is the mental shift, *UI as a function of state*, and it is the single most important idea in modern frontend, because it makes complex, dynamic interfaces tractable by removing the manual DOM-syncing that made them so error-prone. Everything in React (and its successors) flows from this: describe the UI for the data, let the framework sync the DOM.

## Where this fits
This opens the **Frontend phase** (W5-8): React (the component model, this week), then Next.js (the production React framework, W6), Tailwind (styling, W7), and state management (W8), the frontend stack most jobs use. It builds directly on the component thinking from Astro, now made interactive and declarative. Today's orientation: React is the component mental model plus a declarative paradigm, you describe the UI as a function of data (props/state) and React syncs the DOM, eliminating the imperative DOM-juggling of weeks 1-2. Tomorrow you build React components.

items.title: State
items.body:
## State: data that changes over time
Props are inputs from above; **state** is data a component *owns and changes over time*, and it is what makes components interactive. When a user clicks, types, or toggles, you update state, and React re-renders to reflect it. The hook for state is `useState`:
```jsx
import { useState } from 'react';
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);          // state variable + its setter
  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>   // update state on click
      Clicked {count} times
    </button>
  );
}
```
`useState(0)` gives you the current value (`count`) and a function to change it (`setCount`). Crucially, you *never* mutate state directly (`count = 5` does nothing useful), you call the setter (`setCount(5)`), which tells React the state changed so it re-renders the component with the new value. This is the declarative model in action: you change the *state*, and React updates the *DOM* to match, you never touch the DOM yourself.

## The core loop: state changes, UI re-renders
The single most important idea in React is the render loop, and `useState` makes it concrete: **when state changes, React re-runs the component function and updates the DOM to match the new output.**
```text
1. component renders with current state (count = 0) -> button shows "Clicked 0 times"
2. user clicks -> setCount(1) -> React knows state changed
3. React RE-RENDERS: re-runs the function with count = 1 -> "Clicked 1 times"
4. React updates only the changed part of the DOM
```
This is *UI as a function of state*, realised: your component describes what the UI looks like for the current state, and every time state changes, React re-derives the UI and syncs the DOM. You do not manually update the button text, you update the state, and the re-render handles the DOM. This loop, **state -> render -> state changes -> re-render**, is the engine of every React app, and internalising it is the key to thinking in React: you stop asking "what DOM changes do I make?" and start asking "what is my state, and what should the UI look like for it?" Everything interactive, a toggle, a form, a live filter, a loaded list, is just state changing and the UI re-rendering to match.

## State rules and lifting state up
Two essential disciplines around state:
- **Treat state as immutable, update via the setter.** Never modify state directly; always call the setter with the new value. For objects and arrays, create a *new* one rather than mutating the old (`setItems([...items, newItem])`, not `items.push(...)`), because React detects changes by comparing references, so mutating in place can fail to trigger a re-render, a classic, baffling beginner bug. Always produce new state, never edit existing state in place.
- **Lift state up when it's shared.** State lives in a component, but when *two* components need the same state (a filter control and the list it filters), you **lift the state up** to their nearest common parent and pass it down to both via props (and pass a setter function down so a child can update it). This keeps the one-way data flow intact: shared state lives in a common ancestor and flows down to everyone who needs it. Knowing *where* state should live, as low as possible, but high enough to be shared by all who need it, is a core React design skill, and "lifting state up" is the standard answer to "two components need to share data." (When lifting gets painful across many layers, that is the problem state-management libraries solve, W8.)

## Where this fits
You understand state: a component's own changeable data via `useState`, driving the core render loop (state changes -> re-render -> DOM syncs), with the rules of immutable updates and lifting shared state to a common parent. State is what makes components interactive. Tomorrow you meet refs, for the cases where you need to step outside the declarative model and touch the DOM directly.

items.title: Refs
items.body:
## Refs: an escape hatch to the DOM
React's declarative model (describe UI from state, let React handle the DOM) covers almost everything, but occasionally you genuinely need a *direct handle* to a DOM element, to focus an input, measure an element's size, play a video, or integrate a non-React library, and **refs** are the escape hatch for that. A ref gives you a stable reference to a DOM node (or any value that persists across renders without triggering one):
```jsx
import { useRef } from 'react';
function SearchBox() {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);
  return (
    <>
      <input ref={inputRef} />
      <button onClick={() => inputRef.current.focus()}>Focus the input</button>
    </>
  );
}
```
`useRef` creates a ref, you attach it to an element with `ref={inputRef}`, and `inputRef.current` is then the actual DOM node, which you can call methods on (`.focus()`, `.play()`, measure, etc.).

## When refs are appropriate (and when they're not)
The discipline with refs is knowing they are a *deliberate exception* to the declarative model, to be used sparingly and only when state cannot do the job. The rule of thumb:
- **Use state** for anything that affects *what the UI renders*, the displayed value, whether something is shown, the list of items. This is the normal, declarative path, and it is right the vast majority of the time.
- **Use a ref** only for things *outside* React's rendering that you cannot express as state: imperatively focusing or scrolling to an element, measuring its actual size/position, controlling media playback, or holding a value that should persist across renders *without* causing a re-render (like a timer id).
The anti-pattern to avoid is using refs to *manipulate the DOM that React manages*, reaching in to change text or styles directly, because that fights React (React will overwrite your changes on the next render, and the DOM and your state get out of sync, exactly the imperative mess React exists to prevent). So refs are for *escaping to* the imperative world for the few things that require it (focus, measure, media, third-party libraries), not for replacing the declarative model. Knowing the boundary, state for what renders, refs only for genuine imperative needs React cannot express, keeps your code clean and declarative while still handling the cases that need direct DOM access.

## Why having an escape hatch matters
The deeper lesson refs teach is a property of well-designed abstractions: **a good abstraction provides an escape hatch for the cases it does not cover.** React's declarative model is powerful but cannot express *everything* (it has no declarative way to say "focus this input now" or "what is this element's pixel height?"), and rather than leaving you stuck, React provides refs as a controlled escape to the underlying imperative DOM for exactly those cases. This is a mark of good design, the abstraction handles the common case beautifully while giving you a clean way down to the lower level when you truly need it, so you are never *trapped* by the abstraction. Recognising this pattern, and using the escape hatch *responsibly* (only when the abstraction genuinely cannot express what you need, not as a way to avoid learning the proper declarative approach), is a valuable engineering instinct that applies far beyond React. The temptation for a beginner is to reach for refs to do things the "old imperative way" they are comfortable with; the discipline is to stay declarative (use state) by default and drop to refs only for the genuine imperative needs, which keeps the benefits of the abstraction while still handling the edge cases. Refs are the well-designed escape hatch, used sparingly and deliberately.

## Where this fits
You understand refs: a deliberate escape hatch to the actual DOM for the few imperative needs (focus, measure, media, third-party libraries) that React's declarative state model cannot express, used sparingly so you stay declarative by default. Tomorrow you handle a very common interactive feature in React: forms.

items.title: Rendering performance
items.body:
## Understanding (and controlling) re-renders
React's render loop, state changes, the component re-runs, is usually fast and you ignore it. But as apps grow, *unnecessary* re-renders can hurt performance, and understanding **when and why React re-renders** is what lets you keep a React app fast. The key facts: a component re-renders when its *state* changes, when its *props* change, or when its *parent* re-renders (which cascades down). That last one surprises people, when a parent re-renders, *all* its children re-render by default, even children whose props did not change, which is usually fine (React is fast) but can become wasteful in large trees or with expensive components.
```text
parent re-renders  ->  ALL children re-render by default
  (fine usually; a problem when children are many or expensive)
```

## The tools: memo, useMemo, useCallback
React gives you tools to *skip* unnecessary work, and knowing what each does (and when to use it) is the performance toolkit:
- **`React.memo`** wraps a component so it *skips re-rendering* when its props have not changed (a shallow comparison). Use it on an expensive component that re-renders often with the same props, so it only re-renders when its props actually change, not just because its parent did.
- **`useMemo`** *caches the result of an expensive computation* so it is not recomputed on every render unless its inputs change. Use it for genuinely costly calculations (filtering/sorting a large list, parsing) so they run only when their inputs change.
- **`useCallback`** *caches a function* so it keeps the same reference across renders, which matters when you pass a function as a prop to a `memo`'d child (a new function each render would defeat the `memo`).
These are the standard optimisation hooks, and notice they are the exact tools used to fix a real performance bug in FORGE itself (memoising components so a checkbox toggle did not re-parse markdown and reload an iframe on every render), this is not abstract, it is the everyday craft of keeping interfaces responsive.

## Optimise deliberately, measure first
The crucial discipline, the same as every performance lesson in the track, is **do not optimise prematurely, measure first.** React is fast by default, and the vast majority of components do *not* need `memo`, `useMemo`, or `useCallback`, sprinkling them everywhere adds complexity and can even *hurt* (the memoisation itself has a cost), so they are not free wins to apply reflexively. The right approach: build normally without these optimisations, and reach for them *only* when you have an actual, observed performance problem, a list that lags, a typing input that stutters, a tree that re-renders visibly slowly. Then you **measure** to find the real cause: the React DevTools Profiler shows you *which* components re-render and how long they take, so you can identify the actual expensive, over-rendering component rather than guessing, and apply the right fix (`memo` the expensive child, `useMemo` the costly calculation) to *that* specific spot. This is the same measure-then-optimise rigor as the ML and AI-eng performance work: premature optimisation wastes effort and adds complexity on code that was never slow, while measured optimisation fixes the actual bottleneck. The mature React developer writes clean, simple components by default, profiles when there is a real performance issue, and optimises precisely where the profiler points, not everywhere out of habit. Understanding re-renders lets you *diagnose* performance issues; the optimisation hooks let you *fix* them; and the discipline of measuring first ensures you spend that effort only where it actually helps.

## Where this fits
You understand React rendering performance: what triggers re-renders (state, props, parent), the tools to skip unnecessary work (`React.memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback`), and the discipline of optimising only when you have measured a real problem (via the Profiler), not prematurely. Tomorrow you assemble the week's React skills and ship.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: an interactive React app
You assemble the week into a real interactive React application, perhaps Bean Forge's interactive parts rebuilt in React, or a small app (a menu with live filtering, a cart, a form), demonstrating the component mental model in action:
- **components** composed into a tree, with data flowing down via props.
- **state** (`useState`) driving interactivity through the render loop, lifted appropriately where shared.
- **controlled forms**, a **ref** where genuinely needed, and clean, un-over-optimised rendering (with the performance tools understood for when needed).
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "React app: components, state, forms, the declarative component model"
git push
```

## The deliverable demonstrates thinking in components and state
What makes this project show real React competence is that it demonstrates the *mental model*, not just API usage. The strongest version shows a UI cleanly *decomposed into a tree of focused components*, *interactivity driven by state* through the declarative render loop (you change state, the UI updates, you never touch the DOM imperatively), and the data flowing predictably one way down the tree. If you can look at an interface and naturally see it as a component tree with state living in the right places, and build it that way, you have internalised the thing this week was for. The contrast with weeks 1-2 is the proof: the same interactivity that took manual DOM manipulation (find element, change it, keep it in sync) is now expressed declaratively (describe the UI for the state, let React sync the DOM), which is cleaner, less buggy, and scales. Demonstrating that you *think in components and state*, decompose the UI, own the state, let React render, is the deliverable, because that mental model is what transfers to every framework and every frontend job.

## What React established
Step back: you have learned the mental model that underlies all modern frontend, *interfaces as trees of components, with UI as a declarative function of state.* You can decompose any UI into composable, prop-driven components; you drive interactivity with state through the render loop (state changes, React re-renders, the DOM syncs); you handle forms with controlled inputs; you escape to the DOM with refs when truly needed; and you understand and can control rendering performance. Crucially, because you learned the raw DOM and imperative manipulation *first* (weeks 1-2), you understand what React is *doing for you*, replacing manual DOM-syncing with a declarative model, which makes React a comprehensible tool rather than magic. This component-and-state thinking is transferable far beyond React: Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, and the frameworks not yet invented all use a variation of it, so what you learned this week is the durable foundation of frontend, not just one library's API.

## Where this fits
You shipped an interactive React app and internalised the component mental model, interfaces as trees of components with UI as a declarative function of state, the transferable foundation of all modern frontend. Next week you take React to production with **Next.js App Router**, where most frontend jobs are going, adding the server layer (server components, server actions, routing) that makes React apps fast, SEO-friendly, and able to talk to databases securely, the framework that turns React from a client-side library into a full production stack.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Your expense list has a deleteExpense function that removes an expense by id. You pass this function as a prop to each ExpenseItem component: <ExpenseItem onDelete={deleteExpense}>. In the ExpenseItem component, you call props.onDelete(expense.id) when the delete button is clicked. Why pass the function as a prop rather than defining it inside ExpenseItem? ExpenseItem does not own the expenses array, the parent component does. Only the owner of the state should modify it. ExpenseItem is a presentational component: it displays data and signals intent (the user wants to delete this expense), but the actual deletion happens in the parent, which has access to the expenses array and its setter function. This is the one-directional data flow principle: data flows down (expenses passed to ExpenseItem as props), events bubble up (onDelete callback called by ExpenseItem, handled by parent).

weeks.title: Next.js App Router, Where Most Frontend Jobs Are Going
weeks.context:
Next.js App Router is where the industry is going. It builds on React but adds file-based routing, server components, server actions, and built-in optimisations for production. Most new React applications, and most job postings for React roles, are App Router. Understanding why it exists requires understanding the problem it solves: React alone is a client-side library. Next.js adds the server layer that makes React applications SEO-friendly, fast on first load, and capable of accessing databases and secrets without exposing them to the browser.

Server components are the conceptual shift. In React, all components run in the browser. In Next.js App Router, components are server components by default, they run on the server at request time (or build time), have access to the filesystem and environment variables, and send HTML to the browser. The browser receives rendered HTML rather than JavaScript that must first execute before the user sees anything. Client components (marked with 'use client') run in the browser and can use useState, useEffect, and event handlers. The division is not arbitrary, it is the architecture that enables fast initial loads with interactive islands.

The directory you build this week uses MDX, a superset of Markdown that allows you to embed React components in your content. A directory entry can include a live code demo, an interactive chart, or a signup form embedded in the prose. This is impossible with plain Markdown and expensive to implement without a framework like Next.js that handles the compilation.

File-based routing in App Router is folder-based: src/app/page.tsx is the homepage, src/app/directory/page.tsx is /directory, src/app/directory/[slug]/page.tsx handles /directory/any-post-slug. The folder names match the URL segments. Dynamic routes use square brackets. Route groups (folders in parentheses) affect the folder structure without affecting the URL.

Deploying to Vercel is the natural endpoint for Next.js, Vercel created Next.js. The integration is tight: push to GitHub, Vercel builds and deploys automatically. Edge functions, preview deployments for PRs, and analytics are available out of the box.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Next.js: React for production, where the jobs are
React alone is a *client-side* library, it runs in the browser. **Next.js App Router** adds the *server layer* that turns React into a full production framework, and it is where the industry is going: most new React applications, and most React job postings, are App Router. It builds on the React you just learned and adds file-based routing, **server components**, **server actions**, and built-in production optimisations. Understanding *why* Next.js exists is understanding what plain React lacks: React in the browser cannot easily be SEO-friendly, cannot be fast on first load, and cannot safely access databases or secrets (anything in the browser is exposed to users). Next.js adds a server that solves all three, making React applications production-grade. This is also FORGE's own stack, so this week is directly relevant to real work.

## The conceptual shift: server components
The central new idea is the **server component**, and it is a genuine shift from plain React. In React, *all* components run in the browser. In Next.js App Router, components are **server components by default**: they run on the *server* (at request time or build time), have access to the filesystem, databases, and environment variables (secrets), and send finished *HTML* to the browser rather than JavaScript that builds the UI client-side.
```text
plain React:        all components run in the BROWSER (client-side)
Next.js default:    components run on the SERVER -> send HTML to the browser
                    (can read databases & secrets; browser gets rendered HTML)
```
This means a server component can, for example, query a database *directly* (the query runs on the server, the secret connection string never reaches the browser) and send the rendered result as HTML, which plain client-side React cannot do safely. Server components are the foundation of why Next.js is fast (HTML on first load), SEO-friendly (search engines get rendered HTML), and secure (server-only code stays on the server).

## What Next.js adds, at a glance
Beyond server components, Next.js provides the pieces a production React app needs, which you build this week:
- **File-based routing:** files in the `app/` directory define your URLs (like Astro's routing), with support for dynamic routes (`/blog/[slug]`).
- **Server actions:** call server-side functions directly from your components (for mutations like form submissions) without manually building API endpoints.
- **Route handlers:** when you *do* need a traditional API endpoint, you write one.
- **Streaming and Suspense:** send the page progressively so users see content fast even when some parts are slow.
- **Built-in optimisations:** image optimisation, code splitting, caching, all configured for production by default.
Together these make Next.js a complete framework for building fast, SEO-friendly, secure, production React applications, which is exactly why it dominates React hiring.

## Where this fits
This week takes React to production with Next.js App Router, the framework most React jobs now use (and FORGE's stack), adding the server layer that makes React apps fast, SEO-friendly, and database-capable. It builds on last week's React and bridges toward the Backend phase (W9-12), since server components and server actions are your first server-side code. Today's orientation: Next.js adds a server layer to React, with server components (run on the server, access databases/secrets, send HTML) as the key shift that makes React production-grade. Tomorrow you dig into server vs client components, the most important distinction in the App Router.

items.title: Dynamic routes
items.body:
## Dynamic routes: pages from data Most real apps have pages whose content depends on the URL, a blog post at `/blog/my-first-post`, a product at `/products/latte`, a user at `/users/42`, and you cannot write a separate file for every one. **Dynamic routes** handle this: a folder named with brackets, `[slug]`, matches *any* value in that URL position and passes it to the page: ```text app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx -> matches /blog/anything ``` ```jsx async function BlogPost({ params }) { const post = await getPost(params.slug); // params.slug = "my-first-post" return

{post.title}

...
; } ``` The `[slug]` part of the path becomes available as `params.slug`, so *one* file handles *every* blog post: it reads the slug from the URL, fetches that specific post's data (on the server, since it is a server component), and renders it. One template, infinite pages, driven by data and the URL. ## How dynamic routing connects URL, data, and page Dynamic routes teach how a modern app maps *URLs to data to rendered pages*, which is the heart of how content-driven sites work: - The **URL** carries the identifier (the slug, the id) of *what* to show. - The **dynamic route file** (`[slug]/page.tsx`) catches that identifier as `params`. - The **server component** uses it to *fetch the specific data* (this post, this product) directly from the database or CMS. - It **renders** that data into the page, sent as HTML. This URL -> params -> data fetch -> render flow is exactly how you build any catalog, blog, or detail-page-driven app, and because the fetch happens in a server component, it is fast (server-rendered HTML), SEO-friendly (each post has a real, crawlable URL with real content), and secure (the database query stays on the server). You also handle the cases: a slug that does not exist should render a "not found" page (Next.js has a `notFound()` for this), and you can pre-generate pages for known slugs at build time (`generateStaticParams`) for even faster delivery. Understanding dynamic routes is understanding how one piece of code serves a whole collection of data-driven pages, the foundation of content-heavy applications. ## Why this matters: scalable, SEO-friendly content The significance of dynamic routes is that they make content *scale* while staying *discoverable*, which is exactly what plain client-side React struggles with. With a dynamic route, adding the thousandth blog post requires *zero* new code, it is just another row of data that the `[slug]` page renders, so your codebase stays tiny while your content grows arbitrarily. And because each post is server-rendered at its own real URL, search engines can crawl and index every one (real HTML content at a real URL), which is critical for any content site's discoverability, the SEO benefit that pure client-side React (where content is built in the browser after load, often invisible to crawlers) cannot easily match. This is a concrete payoff of the server-component model from yesterday: dynamic routes + server rendering give you data-driven pages that are both infinitely scalable (one template, all the data) and fully SEO-friendly (real URLs with real rendered content), which is why Next.js is the choice for content-rich, discoverable applications. The combination, file-based dynamic routing, server-side data fetching, and HTML output, is the production pattern for building anything from a blog to an e-commerce catalog, and it scales from one page to millions without changing the code. ## Where this fits You can build dynamic routes (`[slug]`) that map a URL to a parameter to a server-side data fetch to a rendered page, serving an entire collection of content from one template, infinitely scalable and fully SEO-friendly. Tomorrow you handle *changing* data, not just displaying it, with server actions for mutations like form submissions.

items.title: Route Handlers
items.body:
## Route handlers: building real API endpoints
Server actions handle your app's internal mutations, but sometimes you need a genuine **HTTP API endpoint**, a stable URL that responds to requests, for a mobile app, a webhook, a third-party service, or any non-React-UI client. **Route handlers** are how you build those in Next.js: a `route.ts` file that exports functions named for HTTP methods:
```jsx
// app/api/menu/route.ts  ->  the URL /api/menu
export async function GET() {
  const items = await db.menu.findMany();
  return Response.json(items);               // respond with JSON
}
export async function POST(request) {
  const data = await request.json();         // read the request body
  const item = await db.menu.create({ data });
  return Response.json(item, { status: 201 });
}
```
This creates a real API at `/api/menu`: a GET returns the menu as JSON, a POST creates an item. Any client, your React UI, a mobile app, `curl`, another server, can call it over HTTP.

## Route handlers are the standard web API model
Route handlers teach the *traditional, universal* API model, which is the same request/response contract you met with native forms (W3) and will design properly in W11, and which works the same in every backend framework (Express, Flask, anything):
- a **URL** (the file path, `/api/menu`) identifies the resource.
- **HTTP methods** map to operations: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (remove), the standard verbs.
- the handler **reads the request** (body, query params, headers) and **returns a response** (JSON data plus a status code).
This is the same HTTP request/response model from the very first week (the browser requests, the server responds), now you are writing the *server* side of it, your first real backend code. It is also exactly the model you will deepen in the Backend phase: REST API design (W11) is about doing this *well* (good URLs, right methods, proper status codes), and the Node/Express week (W9) builds the same kind of endpoints in the dedicated backend framework. So route handlers are both immediately useful (real API endpoints in your Next.js app) and a bridge into backend development, the same HTTP-endpoint model that all server-side web work uses.

## Server actions vs route handlers: completing the picture
With both in hand, you can place the full picture of how a Next.js app handles server-side work, which is the architectural understanding this week builds toward:
- **Server components** (D2): fetch and render data on the server (reads, for display).
- **Server actions** (D4): mutate data from *your own* UI with minimal boilerplate (writes, internal, the common case).
- **Route handlers** (today): real HTTP API endpoints for *external* clients or when you need a standard API contract (reads and writes, for consumers beyond your UI).
The judgement is to reach for the right one: server components to *show* data, server actions for *your app's* mutations, route handlers when you are building an *API others consume*. Using a route handler where a server action would do adds unnecessary API boilerplate for an internal form; using a server action where you need a public API does not work (external clients need a real endpoint). Knowing this, and that all of them run your server-side code securely (database access, secrets, on the server, never exposed to the browser), is the architectural literacy that lets you build a complete Next.js application correctly. The App Router gives you these three complementary tools for server-side work, and choosing among them deliberately is the skill. For most internal app needs, server components + server actions suffice; route handlers are for when you genuinely need a standard API surface.

## Where this fits
You can build route handlers, real HTTP API endpoints (`route.ts`, methods like GET/POST, request in, JSON response out), for external clients or standard API contracts, the universal request/response model that bridges into backend development. You now have the full App Router server toolkit (components, actions, handlers) and know which to use when. Tomorrow you handle making pages feel fast even when data is slow: streaming and Suspense.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a production Next.js app
You assemble the week into a Next.js App Router application, demonstrating the production React stack, perhaps Bean Forge rebuilt as a dynamic app, or a new data-driven project:
- **server components** fetching and rendering data (with secure database/secret access), small **client component** islands for interactivity.
- **dynamic routes** serving a collection of data-driven, SEO-friendly pages.
- **server actions** for the app's mutations (forms, updates), and **route handlers** where a real API is needed.
- **streaming/Suspense** so the page is fast even when some data is slow.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Next.js App Router app: server components, dynamic routes, server actions, streaming"
git push   # deploy to Vercel (Next.js's home) or similar
```

## The deliverable shows production React architecture
What makes this project demonstrate real Next.js competence is the *architecture*, correctly placing the server/client boundary and choosing the right tool for each job. The strongest version shows a mostly-server-component app (fast, SEO-friendly, secure data access) with interactivity isolated to small client islands, data-driven pages via dynamic routes, mutations handled cleanly with server actions, and slow parts streamed with Suspense, all the App Router pieces used *appropriately*. The proof is that the app is genuinely production-grade: it loads fast (server-rendered HTML, streaming), it is SEO-friendly (real URLs with real content), it accesses data securely (server-side, secrets never exposed), and it is interactive where needed. Being able to *reason about where code runs* (this is a server component because it fetches data; this is a client component because it needs state; this mutation is a server action because it is internal; this is a route handler because an external client calls it) is exactly the architectural understanding that distinguishes someone who can build a real Next.js app from someone who copies snippets, and it is precisely what the App Router jobs require.

## What Next.js established
Step back: you have learned the production React framework that most of the industry is moving to (and that FORGE itself uses). You understand the foundational shift, server components by default, with client islands for interactivity, and the full toolkit it enables: dynamic routes (scalable, SEO-friendly data-driven pages), server actions (low-boilerplate internal mutations), route handlers (real APIs for external clients), and streaming/Suspense (fast, resilient loading). Crucially, you can *reason about where code runs and why*, the server/client boundary, which is the central skill of the App Router and the thing that makes everything else, performance, SEO, security, fall into place. This builds on your React foundation (the components and state are the same; Next.js adds where they run and how data flows) and bridges into the backend (server components and route handlers are real server-side code, your first steps into the full-stack work ahead). You can now build fast, SEO-friendly, secure, production-grade React applications, which is exactly what most frontend roles now demand.

## Where this fits
You shipped a production Next.js App Router app and can reason about the server/client boundary that defines it, the framework where most React jobs are going and FORGE's own stack. Next week you make it *beautiful, fast*, with **Tailwind CSS and design systems**, a utility-first styling approach and a component-library ecosystem (shadcn/ui, Radix) that lets you build polished, consistent, accessible interfaces quickly, the styling layer that turns functional apps into professional-looking products.

weeks.title: Tailwind CSS and Design Systems, Building Beautiful Fast
weeks.context:
Tailwind CSS is a different philosophy from traditional CSS. Instead of writing semantic class names (.hero-section, .card-header) and adding styles in a separate CSS file, Tailwind provides hundreds of small utility classes that you compose directly in your HTML. The hero section might have: className="relative flex items-center justify-center bg-slate-900 px-6 py-24 text-center md:py-36". This looks verbose but produces faster iteration: you never leave the HTML file to style a component, you never deal with naming conventions or specificity conflicts, and you have a constrained design system built in, 8-point spacing scale, curated color palette, responsive prefixes.

The constrained design system is Tailwind's most underrated feature. When you choose between padding-top: 16px and padding-top: 18px, you are making a visual decision with no guidance. When your options are py-4 (16px) and py-5 (20px), the constraint forces consistent spacing. The 8-point grid (4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24...) emerges naturally from Tailwind's spacing scale. The result: your components look cohesive even before you have a design system, because they are all using the same underlying scale.

Building a UI kit this week means building components that other components will use: a Button that has primary/secondary/danger variants, a Card with an optional header and footer, a Badge for status indicators, an Alert for informational messages, a Table for data display. Each component accepts props that control its variant and renders the appropriate Tailwind classes.

The class merging problem appears quickly: if your Button component has base classes and you pass a className prop with additional classes, they must be merged correctly. conflicting classes (bg-blue-500 from the component, bg-red-500 from the caller) must be resolved. The clsx and tailwind-merge libraries handle this, clsx provides conditional class joining, tailwind-merge resolves Tailwind-specific conflicts.

Dark mode in Tailwind uses the dark: prefix. Every class can be conditionally applied in dark mode: dark:bg-slate-800 dark:text-white. Tailwind's dark mode can be configured as class-based (adds dark when .dark is on the html element) or media-based (respects the OS preference). Class-based dark mode gives you user control; media-based is automatic.

## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for free, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Tailwind: a different philosophy of styling
You styled with traditional CSS in week one, semantic class names (`.hero-section`) and rules in a separate file. **Tailwind CSS** takes a different, initially-surprising approach: instead of writing class names and separate CSS, you compose hundreds of small **utility classes** directly in your markup, each doing one tiny thing:
```jsx
<section className="relative flex items-center justify-center bg-slate-900 px-6 py-24 text-center md:py-36">
```
That `className` reads as: positioned relative, flexbox centering its items, dark background, horizontal padding 6, vertical padding 24 (more on medium screens and up), centered text. It looks verbose, even ugly at first, but it produces *faster iteration*: you never leave the markup file to style something, you never invent class names or fight CSS specificity conflicts, and you get a *constrained design system* built in. This week you learn Tailwind and the component ecosystem (shadcn/ui, Radix) that, together, are how modern polished UIs are built fast, and it is FORGE's styling approach too.

## Why utilities beat hand-written CSS for iteration
The case for Tailwind is about *development speed and maintainability at scale*, and understanding it dissolves the initial "this looks wrong" reaction:
- **No context switching:** you style right in the markup, never jumping to a separate CSS file and back, so building and adjusting a component is one continuous flow.
- **No naming:** you do not invent (and later decipher) class names like `.card-header-inner-wrapper`, naming things is genuinely hard, and utilities skip it entirely.
- **No specificity wars:** traditional CSS at scale produces specificity conflicts (this rule overrides that one unexpectedly) and dead CSS (styles no one knows if they can delete); utilities, applied directly to elements, sidestep both, what you see in the markup is exactly what applies.
- **Co-location:** the styling lives *with* the element, so deleting a component deletes its styles (no orphaned CSS), and understanding an element's appearance means reading its classes, not hunting through stylesheets.
The verbosity is the trade for these benefits, and in practice (especially with components, where you write the markup once and reuse it) the speed and maintainability win out, which is why Tailwind became dominant for app development.

## The underrated superpower: a constrained design system
Tailwind's *most underrated* feature, and the deepest reason it produces good-looking results fast, is its **constrained design system**. When you write raw CSS and must choose between `padding-top: 16px` and `padding-top: 18px`, you are making a visual decision with *no guidance*, and a thousand such tiny ungrounded choices produce subtle inconsistency (slightly different spacings, a dozen almost-same blues). Tailwind constrains you to a *curated scale*: spacing is an 8-point system (`p-4` is 16px, `p-6` is 24px, no in-between to agonise over), colours come from a designed palette (`slate-900`, `blue-500`), and there are sensible defaults for typography, shadows, and radii. By choosing from a *limited, harmonious set* of options rather than arbitrary values, your design comes out consistent and balanced *by default*, the constraint removes the infinite-choice paralysis and the inconsistency it breeds. This is the same idea as the "use a defined palette and spacing scale" discipline from week one, now *enforced* by the tool: Tailwind makes the consistent choice the easy choice, which is why even non-designers produce more cohesive UIs with it. The constraint is a feature, not a limitation.

## Where this fits
This week is the styling layer of the Frontend phase: Tailwind (utility-first CSS with a built-in design system) plus the component ecosystem (shadcn/ui, Radix UI, motion), how modern polished, consistent, accessible UIs are built quickly, and FORGE's own approach. It builds on your CSS fundamentals (Tailwind is CSS, just composed differently) and your React components (utilities shine with reusable components). Today's orientation: Tailwind composes small utility classes in the markup for faster iteration, no naming or specificity fights, and a constrained design system that makes consistent design the default. Tomorrow you learn Tailwind's core.

items.title: Dark mode patterns
items.body:
## Dark mode, done properly
You built a basic dark mode in week 2; now you do it the modern, robust way with Tailwind's `dark:` variant. Tailwind makes the *styling* trivial, every element just gets its dark variant inline:
```jsx
<div className="bg-white text-slate-900 dark:bg-slate-900 dark:text-white">
<button className="bg-blue-500 dark:bg-blue-400 hover:bg-blue-600 dark:hover:bg-blue-500">
```
The `dark:` prefix applies when dark mode is active, so a single element declares both its light and dark appearance right where it lives. Dark mode is toggled by a `dark` class on a root element (Tailwind's `class` strategy), so adding/removing `dark` on `<html>` flips the whole UI between the light and dark variants you declared, the same class-toggling idea from week 2, now powering a complete theme system with minimal effort.

## The hard parts: persistence and the flash
Tailwind handles the styling, but the *robust* parts of dark mode are the ones you met as challenges in week 2, now to be solved properly:
- **Persistence:** the user's choice must survive reloads, stored (localStorage) and re-applied, exactly as in week 2.
- **System preference:** respect the user's OS-level setting (`prefers-color-scheme`) as the default, so a user whose system is in dark mode sees dark mode without toggling, a real consideration, defaulting to the system preference and letting the user override it.
- **The flash (FOUC):** the critical hard part, if you apply the saved theme with JavaScript *after* the page renders, dark-mode users see a flash of light theme first (the week-2 problem). In a Next.js/SSR context this is *more* pronounced, because the server renders the page without knowing the user's theme, so it can send light HTML that then flips to dark on the client. The proper fix is to apply the theme class *before* the page paints, typically a tiny blocking script in the `<head>` that reads the saved/system preference and sets the `dark` class synchronously before the body renders, so the correct theme is present from the very first paint, no flash.
Solving these, persistence, system-preference default, and especially the no-flash application, is what separates a polished dark mode from a janky one.

## Why dark mode teaches real production concerns
Dark mode is a great teacher because it surfaces *real production concerns* that go beyond "make it look right," and these concerns recur throughout serious frontend work:
- **The loading/hydration experience:** the flash problem is fundamentally about *what the user sees during loading and the transition from server HTML to client JavaScript*, which is a central concern in SSR frameworks like Next.js (the broader topic of "hydration"). Getting dark mode's first paint right trains you to think about the *initial render and the server-to-client handoff*, not just the final state.
- **Respecting user preferences:** honouring `prefers-color-scheme` (and `prefers-reduced-motion` from week 2) is part of building software that *respects the user's stated choices*, a real responsibility and accessibility concern.
- **State that spans client and server:** the theme is a piece of state that must be consistent across the server render and the client, a microcosm of the broader challenge of managing state in SSR apps.
So while dark mode seems like a cosmetic feature, building it *properly*, persistent, system-aware, flash-free, teaches the production-grade thinking about loading experience, server/client consistency, and user preferences that distinguishes professional frontend work. Tailwind makes the styling easy; the *engineering* of doing it right is the real lesson, and it is exactly the kind of detail that, done well, makes an app feel polished and considered.

## Where this fits
You can build dark mode properly: Tailwind's `dark:` variant for trivial styling, plus the robust engineering, persistence, system-preference default, and a flash-free first paint (especially important in SSR), which teaches real production concerns about loading experience, server/client consistency, and respecting user preferences. Tomorrow you accelerate UI building dramatically with shadcn/ui.

items.title: shadcn/ui
items.body:
## shadcn/ui: high-quality components you own
Building every component from scratch (buttons, dialogs, dropdowns, forms) is slow, and reinventing well-solved UI is wasteful. **shadcn/ui** is a different, increasingly-dominant approach to a component library: instead of installing a package you import from, you *copy the component's code into your project* and own it. You run a command, and the component's source (built with Tailwind and Radix primitives) is added to your codebase:
```bash
npx shadcn@latest add button dialog dropdown-menu
# -> adds button.tsx, dialog.tsx, etc. into YOUR components folder
```
Now you have a beautifully-styled, accessible `<Button>`, `<Dialog>`, etc., as *your own files* that you can read, customise, and adapt freely, no fighting a library's API to change a style, you just edit the code. This "copy, don't install" model is why shadcn/ui took over: you get the speed of a component library with the freedom of owning the code.

## Why "own the code" is the winning model
The shadcn approach solves the central tension of component libraries, and understanding the trade-off it resolves clarifies why it is so popular:
- **Traditional component libraries** (you install and import) give you components fast, but you are *locked into their styling and API*: customising deeply means fighting the library (overriding styles, working around its props), and you cannot easily change behaviour the library did not expose. You move fast until you need something the library does not bend to.
- **Building from scratch** gives total control but is slow and error-prone (especially the accessibility, which is genuinely hard, as tomorrow shows).
- **shadcn/ui** gives you *both*: the components are copied into your project as editable code built on solid foundations (Tailwind styling you can tweak, Radix accessibility you get for free), so you start fast *and* retain full control, because the code is *yours*. Need the dialog to behave differently? Edit the file. Want a different style? Change the classes. There is no library API to fight, because there is no library, just code you own.
This is a genuinely better trade for app development, and it pairs perfectly with Tailwind (the components *are* styled with Tailwind utilities you already understand, so customising them is just editing Tailwind classes you can read). It is FORGE's approach and the modern default for React apps that want polished components without lock-in.

## Use it as a foundation, not a crutch
The discipline with shadcn/ui (and any component source you adopt) is to use it as a *well-built foundation you understand and adapt*, not a black box you paste blindly. Because the code is in your project, you *can and should* read it, understanding how the components are built (their use of Radix primitives for behaviour, Tailwind for style) teaches you good component patterns and accessibility practices, so adopting shadcn components is also a *learning* opportunity, not just a shortcut. You then adapt them to your design (your colours, your spacing, your specific needs) rather than using them stock, which is the whole point of owning the code. The trap to avoid is treating it as magic to copy-paste without comprehension, which leaves you stuck when you need to change something and unable to debug when something breaks. Used well, shadcn/ui dramatically speeds up building polished, accessible UIs (you are not reinventing the dialog or the dropdown) *while* keeping you in control and teaching you how good components are made, which is exactly the right balance of leverage and understanding. It exemplifies a great pattern: stand on solid, well-made foundations, but *own and understand* them so you are never trapped. For building real app UIs fast and well, shadcn/ui plus Tailwind is a powerful combination, and one you will use constantly.

## Where this fits
You understand shadcn/ui: high-quality, accessible, Tailwind-styled components *copied into your project as code you own*, giving the speed of a library with the freedom and learning of owning the source, the modern default (and FORGE's). It is built on Radix primitives, which you go deeper on tomorrow, the accessibility engine underneath.

items.title: Radix UI primitives
items.body:
## Radix UI: the hard parts of accessible components
shadcn/ui's components are built on **Radix UI primitives**, and understanding Radix reveals *why* those components are good: Radix provides the **behaviour and accessibility** of complex interactive components (dropdowns, dialogs, tooltips, tabs, comboboxes) *without* any styling, so you (or shadcn) add the styling on top. Radix gives you a dropdown that *works correctly* and is *fully accessible*, and you make it *look* however you want:
```text
Radix primitive (Dropdown): handles keyboard nav, focus management, ARIA roles,
                            click-outside-to-close, escape-to-close, screen-reader support
You / shadcn:               add the Tailwind styling on top
```
The split is deliberate: behaviour and accessibility are the *hard, universal* parts (the same for every dropdown), so Radix solves them once, correctly, while styling is the *custom* part, so it is left to you.

## Why accessible interactive components are genuinely hard
The reason Radix exists, and the real lesson here, is that building accessible interactive components *correctly* is *much* harder than it looks, and getting it wrong excludes real users. Consider a "simple" dropdown menu, to be correct and accessible it must: open and close on click *and* keyboard, trap and manage focus (focus moves into the menu when open, returns sensibly when closed), support full keyboard navigation (arrow keys to move between items, Enter to select, Escape to close, type-ahead to jump to an item), have correct ARIA roles and attributes so screen readers announce it properly, close when you click outside or press Escape, and handle edge cases (positioning so it does not go off-screen, etc.). That is a *lot* of subtle, easy-to-get-wrong behaviour, and most hand-rolled dropdowns get much of it wrong, they work with a mouse but are unusable by keyboard or screen-reader users, silently excluding people who rely on those. Radix implements all of this correctly, so a Radix-based dropdown is keyboard-navigable, screen-reader-friendly, and robust *by default*. This is why you do not build these from scratch: the accessibility and interaction complexity is enormous and you will get it wrong, whereas Radix (and shadcn on top of it) gives you correct, accessible behaviour as a foundation.

## The deep lesson: accessibility is not optional, and is hard
Radix teaches two things that matter beyond the library. First, **accessibility is a real, non-optional responsibility** that runs through this whole track (semantic HTML in W1, labels in W3, focus states in W3, reduced-motion in W2, system preferences in W7), and interactive components are where it is *hardest* to get right, so leaning on accessibility-correct primitives like Radix is how you *actually* ship accessible complex UI rather than just intending to. A keyboard-only user or a screen-reader user is a real person who cannot use your inaccessible dropdown, and accessibility is also frequently a *legal* requirement, so this is not nice-to-have polish, it is correctness for a portion of your users. Second, Radix exemplifies a powerful engineering pattern: **separate the hard, universal concern (behaviour + accessibility) from the custom concern (styling), and solve the hard part once, reusably.** This separation is why the shadcn/Radix/Tailwind stack works so well, Radix handles the brutal accessibility-and-interaction logic universally, Tailwind handles the custom styling, and shadcn glues them into components you own. Recognising that the *behaviour and accessibility* of interactive components is the genuinely hard, get-it-wrong-and-exclude-users part, and that the right move is to build on primitives that solve it correctly rather than reinventing it badly, is the key judgement. You *could* learn to build all this accessibility yourself (and understanding what Radix does for you is valuable), but in practice you build on Radix-based components because correct accessibility is too hard and too important to reinvent per project. For building real, accessible, interactive UIs, the Radix-powered approach is how it is done.

## Where this fits
You understand Radix UI primitives: the *behaviour and accessibility* of complex interactive components (keyboard nav, focus management, ARIA, edge cases) provided correctly and unstyled, so you add styling on top, the hard-and-universal part solved once. This teaches that accessibility is non-optional and genuinely hard, and that building on accessibility-correct primitives is how you actually ship accessible UI. Tomorrow you add motion and polish with Framer Motion.

items.title: Framer Motion / Motion One
items.body:
## Motion that elevates: Framer Motion
You added basic CSS animation in week 2; **Framer Motion** (now "Motion") is the React library for richer, declarative animation, animating components naturally as part of your React code. Instead of manually managing CSS transitions and triggering classes, you declare how a component should animate:
```jsx
import { motion } from 'framer-motion';
<motion.div
  initial={{ opacity: 0, y: 20 }}      // start state
  animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }}        // animate to this
  transition={{ duration: 0.3 }}>
  Bean Forge's daily special
</motion.div>
```
You describe the *start*, the *end*, and the *transition*, and Framer Motion handles the animation, in the same declarative spirit as React itself (you describe the desired animation states, the library does the work). It shines at the things plain CSS struggles with: animating elements as they *enter and leave* the DOM (exit animations), coordinated sequences, gesture-driven animation, and animations tied to React state.

## What Framer Motion does that CSS cannot easily
Framer Motion earns its place by handling animation cases that are awkward or impossible with pure CSS, which is the judgement of *when* to reach for it:
- **Enter/exit animations:** animating an element *out* as it is removed (a modal fading away, a list item sliding out before it disappears) is genuinely hard in plain CSS (the element is gone before CSS can animate it), and Framer Motion's `AnimatePresence` handles it cleanly, a major practical win.
- **State-driven and coordinated animation:** animating in response to React state changes, or sequencing multiple elements (a list staggering in), is natural in Framer Motion and fiddly in CSS.
- **Gestures and interaction:** drag, hover, and tap animations with physics-based spring motion that feels natural.
For these, Framer Motion is the right tool. But the *discipline from week 2 still fully applies*: for *simple* animation (a hover effect, a basic transition, a fade), plain CSS is simpler, lighter, and more performant, so you do *not* reach for a JavaScript animation library for things CSS handles fine. Framer Motion is for the richer, harder cases (exit animations, complex state-driven sequences, gestures) where its power is warranted, not a replacement for simple CSS transitions. Knowing the boundary, CSS for simple motion, Framer Motion for the complex/exit/gesture cases, is the practical judgement.

## Restraint and accessibility, still
The most important lesson about animation, established in week 2 and *more* relevant now that you have a powerful animation library, is **restraint and accessibility**, because a powerful tool makes it easier to overdo it. All the week-2 principles hold and matter more:
- **Subtle and purposeful:** richer animation capability is *more* tempting to misuse, so the discipline of subtle, purposeful, fast motion is *more* important, gratuitous, heavy animation everywhere makes an app feel slow and amateurish no matter how impressive the individual effects. Good motion guides and delights quietly; bad motion distracts and annoys. Use Framer Motion's power *sparingly and tastefully*.
- **Accessible:** honour `prefers-reduced-motion`, exactly as in week 2, Framer Motion can respect it (reducing or disabling animation for users who asked for less motion), and you *must* wire this up, because motion sensitivity is a real accessibility concern and a powerful animation library used without this consideration actively harms those users.
- **Performance:** animate the cheap properties (opacity, transform) that the browser handles efficiently, and keep animations fast.
The deeper point is that *more capability demands more discipline*: now that you *can* animate almost anything, the skill is in *what you choose not to animate* and in keeping motion subtle, fast, purposeful, and accessible. The best-animated apps use rich motion *selectively*, a tasteful page transition, a satisfying micro-interaction, an exit animation that adds smoothness, not constant movement. Framer Motion gives you the power; the week-2 discipline of restraint and accessibility is what makes you use it *well*. Polish through motion is real and valuable, but it is achieved through judicious, accessible, purposeful animation, not through animating everything because you can.

## Where this fits
You can add rich animation with Framer Motion (declarative animate states, enter/exit animations, state-driven and gesture motion) for the cases CSS cannot handle easily, while keeping the week-2 discipline, CSS for simple motion, restraint and `prefers-reduced-motion` accessibility throughout, more important now that you have more power. Tomorrow you assemble the week's styling and component skills and ship a polished UI.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a beautiful, fast, accessible UI
You assemble the week into a polished, professional-looking interface, perhaps a redesigned Bean Forge or your Next.js app, styled to a high standard:
- **Tailwind** utilities composing a consistent design (using the constrained system, a custom palette, responsive and dark-mode variants), extracted into reusable components.
- **shadcn/ui** components (owned, customised) for the complex pieces, built on **Radix** primitives for correct accessibility.
- proper **dark mode** (persistent, system-aware, flash-free) and tasteful, accessible **motion** (Framer Motion where warranted, CSS where simple).
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Polished UI: Tailwind design system, shadcn/ui, accessible components, tasteful motion"
git push
```

## The deliverable is polish *and* accessibility *and* speed
What makes this project demonstrate real frontend competence is that it is *beautiful, accessible, and fast, together*, not one at the expense of the others. The strongest version looks genuinely professional (consistent spacing and color from the design system, polished components, tasteful motion), is fully accessible (keyboard-navigable via Radix-based components, proper focus states, honoured motion and color preferences, semantic structure), and is fast (Tailwind's tiny CSS output, CSS for simple animation, no gratuitous motion). That combination is the mark of professional frontend work, because amateurs typically achieve at most one (a pretty app that is inaccessible, or an accessible app that is ugly, or a flashy app that is slow), while the professional standard is *all three*. Demonstrating that you can build interfaces that are visually polished *and* accessible *and* performant, using the modern stack (Tailwind + shadcn/Radix + tasteful motion) the way it is meant to be used, is exactly the deliverable, and it is the styling competence that turns your functional React/Next.js apps into products that look and feel professional.

## What the styling week established
Step back: you can now build *beautiful, consistent, accessible, fast* UIs *quickly*, which is a large part of what makes a frontend developer effective. You learned Tailwind (utility-first styling with a constrained design system that makes consistency the default), the modern component approach (shadcn/ui components you own, built on Radix primitives that solve the hard accessibility correctly), proper dark mode (with its real production concerns), and rich-but-disciplined motion (Framer Motion where warranted, restraint and accessibility throughout). The throughlines are the design-system discipline (constrain your choices for consistency), the accessibility-is-non-optional responsibility (which this stack helps you actually meet), and the "stand on solid foundations you own and understand" pattern (shadcn/Radix). This styling layer, combined with your React (W5) and Next.js (W6), means you can build complete, polished, production-grade frontends, the full modern frontend competence that most jobs require. And it is FORGE's own stack, so it is directly the skill set behind real, shipped products.

## Where this fits
You shipped a beautiful, accessible, fast UI using the modern styling stack (Tailwind, shadcn/ui, Radix, tasteful motion), completing your ability to build polished production frontends. One frontend topic remains before the backend: next week is **state management at scale**, handling state that must be shared across many components (beyond `useState` and prop-drilling), with the right tool for each *kind* of state, server data, global UI state, URL state, form state, the final piece of frontend architecture before you turn to the server side.
